## Load gene annotation maps
```{r}
# Extract GeneID to gene_symbol from NCBI genomic.gff
gff_lines <- readLines("genomic.gff")
gene_lines <- grep("\tgene\t", gff_lines, value = TRUE)

extract_geneid_symbol <- function(attr) {
  id <- sub(".*Dbxref=GeneID:([0-9]+).*", "\\1", attr)
  symbol <- sub(".*;gene=([^;]+);.*", "\\1", attr)
  data.frame(GeneID = id, gene_symbol = symbol)
}

gff_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gene_lines, function(line) {
  fields <- strsplit(line, "\t")[[1]]
  if (length(fields) >= 9) extract_geneid_symbol(fields[9]) else NULL
}))

gff_df$GeneID <- as.character(gff_df$GeneID)


# Combine GFF and gene2ensembl mappings
gene_map <- gff_df %>%
  dplyr::distinct()

## create separate map for manually labeled LOC genes
loc_map <- c(
  "103040661" = "her4.1", #radial glia
  "103035120" = "gfap", #astrocytes/radial glia
  "103034161" = "mpeg1", #macrophage/microglia
  "125803969"= "mrc1b" #macrophage/microglia
)

## update map 
# Make sure GeneID is character to match loc_map names
gene_map$GeneID <- as.character(gene_map$GeneID)

# Replace gene_symbol where GeneID matches your manual map
gene_map$gene_symbol <- ifelse(
  gene_map$GeneID %in% names(loc_map),
  loc_map[gene_map$GeneID],
  gene_map$gene_symbol
)

# Check results
head(gene_map)
```

## define functions
### Run binomial glm for composition stats
Note: scCoda does not work well with low n data sets
Binomial glm with dispersion and batch
-Runs binomial with batch correction first, tests overdispersion vs overdisp_cut, if above threshold, uses beta-binomial for stats
```{r}
run_prop_glm_and_plot <- function(
  denom_obj,
  group_var = "idents",           # "idents" or metadata column in denom_obj
  sample_col = "sample_id",
  pop_col = "population",
  batch_col = "batch",            # created from sample_id if missing
  pop_ref = "surface",
  pop_levels = c("surface", "cave"),
  plot_percent = TRUE,
  bar_error = c("sem", "sd", "none"),
  overlay_points = TRUE,
  point_jitter = 0.08,
  fdr_cutoff = 0.05,
  glm_family = c("auto", "betabinomial", "quasibinomial", "binomial"),
  overdisp_cut = 1.2,
  # ---- batch-driven overdispersion revert gate (AUTO only) ----
  batch_revert = TRUE,
  batch_revert_ratio = 0.6,       # if overdisp_with_batch <= ratio * overdisp_no_batch -> "mostly batch"
  batch_revert_p = 0.05,          # batch must be supported by binomial LRT
  batch_revert_overdisp_max = 1.5,# and residual overdisp w/ batch must be modest
  order_levels = NULL,
  strict_sum_to_one = TRUE
) {
  bar_error  <- match.arg(bar_error)
  glm_family <- match.arg(glm_family)

  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(Seurat)
    library(dplyr)
    library(tidyr)
    library(ggplot2)
    library(purrr)
    library(broom)
  })

  md <- as.data.frame(denom_obj@meta.data)

  if (!all(c(sample_col, pop_col) %in% colnames(md))) {
    stop("Metadata must contain: ", paste(c(sample_col, pop_col), collapse = ", "))
  }

  # unwrap list columns (defensive)
  for (v in c(sample_col, pop_col)) {
    if (is.list(md[[v]])) md[[v]] <- vapply(md[[v]], \(x) as.character(x)[1], character(1))
  }
  if (!identical(group_var, "idents") && group_var %in% colnames(md) && is.list(md[[group_var]])) {
    md[[group_var]] <- vapply(md[[group_var]], \(x) as.character(x)[1], character(1))
  }

  # factorize sample + population
  md[[sample_col]] <- factor(md[[sample_col]])
  md[[pop_col]]    <- stats::relevel(factor(md[[pop_col]], levels = pop_levels), ref = pop_ref)

  # ============================================================
  # Batch: derive from sample_id (underscore => batch2; else batch1)
  # ============================================================
  smp_chr <- as.character(md[[sample_col]])
  md[[batch_col]] <- ifelse(grepl("_", smp_chr), "batch2", "batch1")
  md[[batch_col]] <- factor(md[[batch_col]], levels = c("batch1", "batch2"))

  # group labels from THIS SAME OBJECT
  if (identical(group_var, "idents")) {
    grp <- as.character(Idents(denom_obj))
    default_levels <- levels(Idents(denom_obj))
  } else {
    if (!group_var %in% colnames(md)) stop("group_var not found in metadata: ", group_var)
    grp <- as.character(md[[group_var]])
    default_levels <- if (is.factor(md[[group_var]])) levels(md[[group_var]]) else unique(grp)
  }

  # enforce complete labeling (no silent dropping)
  if (any(is.na(grp) | grp == "")) {
    bad_n <- sum(is.na(grp) | grp == "")
    stop(
      "Found ", bad_n, " cells with NA/blank group labels in ", group_var, ".\n",
      "Fix labels so proportions are well-defined."
    )
  }

  md$.__group <- as.character(grp)

  # determine plotting order
  keep_levels <- if (!is.null(order_levels)) as.character(order_levels) else as.character(default_levels)
  present <- unique(md$.__group)
  if (!all(present %in% keep_levels)) keep_levels <- c(keep_levels, setdiff(present, keep_levels))
  keep_levels <- keep_levels[keep_levels != "" & !is.na(keep_levels)]
  md$.__group <- factor(md$.__group, levels = keep_levels)

  # ============================================================
  # 1) Per-sample counts and proportions
  # ============================================================
  totals <- md %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.data[[sample_col]], .data[[pop_col]], .data[[batch_col]]) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(total = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")

  counts <- md %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.data[[sample_col]], .data[[pop_col]], .data[[batch_col]], .__group) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(count = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")

  props_by_sample <- totals %>%
    tidyr::expand_grid(.__group = factor(keep_levels, levels = keep_levels)) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(counts, by = c(sample_col, pop_col, batch_col, ".__group")) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      count = ifelse(is.na(count), 0L, count),
      non   = total - count,
      prop  = count / total
    )

  if (any(props_by_sample$non < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    stop("Some group counts exceeded totals (should not happen with one input object).")
  }

  qc_sumprop <- props_by_sample %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.data[[sample_col]], .data[[pop_col]], .data[[batch_col]]) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(sum_prop = sum(prop), .groups = "drop")

  if (isTRUE(strict_sum_to_one)) {
    if (any(abs(qc_sumprop$sum_prop - 1) > 1e-6)) {
      print(qc_sumprop)
      stop(
        "Proportions do not sum to 1 within at least one (sample, population, batch).\n",
        "This indicates grouping does not partition all cells in the object."
      )
    }
  }

  # ============================================================
  # 2) Bars + error bars across samples
  # ============================================================
  bar_df <- props_by_sample %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.__group, .data[[pop_col]]) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_prop = mean(prop, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_prop   = sd(prop, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_samp    = dplyr::n(),
      se_prop   = sd_prop / sqrt(n_samp),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      Var1 = factor(as.character(.__group), levels = keep_levels),
      Var2 = factor(as.character(.data[[pop_col]]), levels = pop_levels)
    )

  cellprops <- bar_df %>% dplyr::transmute(Var1, Var2, Freq = mean_prop)

  # ============================================================
  # 3) Effects per group (population cave vs surface)
  # ============================================================
  pop_term <- paste0(pop_col, pop_levels[2])  # e.g. "populationcave"

  # Robust beta-binomial fitter (tries multiple glmmTMBControl settings)
  fit_bb_robust <- function(form, data) {
    if (!requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)) {
      stop("glm_family includes betabinomial but 'glmmTMB' is not installed.")
    }

    ctrl_list <- list(
      glmmTMB::glmmTMBControl(),
      glmmTMB::glmmTMBControl(
        optimizer = stats::nlminb,
        optCtrl = list(iter.max = 100000, eval.max = 100000)
      ),
      glmmTMB::glmmTMBControl(
        optimizer = stats::optim,
        optArgs = list(method = "BFGS"),
        optCtrl = list(maxit = 100000)
      )
    )

    fits <- vector("list", length(ctrl_list))
    diags <- vector("list", length(ctrl_list))

    for (i in seq_along(ctrl_list)) {
      warn_msgs <- character(0)

      fit_i <- tryCatch(
        withCallingHandlers(
          glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
            form,
            family = glmmTMB::betabinomial(link = "logit"),
            data = data,
            control = ctrl_list[[i]]
          ),
          warning = function(w) {
            warn_msgs <<- c(warn_msgs, conditionMessage(w))
            invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
          }
        ),
        error = function(e) NULL
      )

      if (is.null(fit_i)) {
        fits[[i]] <- NULL
        diags[[i]] <- list(ok = FALSE, warn = "ERROR", conv = NA_integer_, pdHess = NA, aic = Inf)
        next
      }

      conv_code <- tryCatch(fit_i$fit$convergence, error = function(e) NA_integer_)
      pdHess    <- tryCatch(isTRUE(fit_i$sdr$pdHess), error = function(e) NA)
      aic_val   <- tryCatch(stats::AIC(fit_i), error = function(e) Inf)

      ok <- isTRUE(pdHess) && (!is.na(conv_code) && conv_code == 0)

      fits[[i]] <- fit_i
      diags[[i]] <- list(
        ok = ok,
        warn = if (length(warn_msgs) > 0) paste(unique(warn_msgs), collapse = " | ") else NA_character_,
        conv = conv_code,
        pdHess = pdHess,
        aic = aic_val
      )

      if (ok) return(list(fit = fit_i, diag = diags[[i]]))
    }

    aic_vec <- vapply(diags, function(d) {
      if (is.null(d) || is.null(d$aic) || !is.finite(d$aic)) Inf else d$aic
    }, numeric(1))

    if (all(is.infinite(aic_vec)) || all(vapply(fits, is.null, logical(1)))) {
      return(list(
        fit = NULL,
        diag = list(ok = FALSE, warn = "ALL_FITS_FAILED", conv = NA_integer_, pdHess = NA, aic = Inf)
      ))
    }

    best_i <- which.min(aic_vec)
    list(fit = fits[[best_i]], diag = diags[[best_i]])
  }

  fit_and_tidy_one <- function(df_sub) {
    form_full <- stats::as.formula(paste0("cbind(count, non) ~ ", pop_col, " + ", batch_col))

    # ---- Always fit binomial baseline (for overdisp diagnostic + binomial output) ----
    m_bin <- stats::glm(form_full, family = stats::binomial(), data = df_sub)
    overdisp_bin <- m_bin$deviance / m_bin$df.residual

    tidy_bin <- broom::tidy(m_bin) %>%
      dplyr::filter(term == pop_term) %>%
      dplyr::transmute(
        term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value,
        dispersion = 1,
        overdisp   = overdisp_bin,
        model_used = "binomial"
      )

    if (nrow(tidy_bin) == 0) {
      tidy_bin <- dplyr::tibble(
        term = pop_term, estimate = NA_real_, std.error = NA_real_,
        statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
        dispersion = 1, overdisp = overdisp_bin,
        model_used = "binomial"
      )
    }

    # If binomial explicitly requested -> return it
    if (glm_family == "binomial") return(tidy_bin)

    # Quasi helper (used for explicit quasi or auto fallback)
    fit_quasi_row <- function(label = "quasibinomial") {
      m_q <- stats::glm(form_full, family = stats::quasibinomial(), data = df_sub)
      disp_q <- summary(m_q)$dispersion
      over_q <- m_q$deviance / m_q$df.residual

      td <- broom::tidy(m_q)
      out <- td %>%
        dplyr::filter(term == pop_term) %>%
        dplyr::transmute(
          term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value,
          dispersion = disp_q,
          overdisp   = over_q,
          model_used = label
        )

      if (nrow(out) == 0) {
        out <- dplyr::tibble(
          term = pop_term, estimate = NA_real_, std.error = NA_real_,
          statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
          dispersion = disp_q, overdisp = over_q,
          model_used = label
        )
      }
      out
    }

    if (glm_family == "quasibinomial") return(fit_quasi_row("quasibinomial"))

    # ============================================================
    # AUTO-only "batch explains overdispersion" revert-to-binomial
    # ============================================================
    if (glm_family == "auto" && isTRUE(batch_revert)) {
      form_nobatch <- stats::as.formula(paste0("cbind(count, non) ~ ", pop_col))
      m_nobatch <- stats::glm(form_nobatch, family = stats::binomial(), data = df_sub)
      overdisp_nobatch <- m_nobatch$deviance / m_nobatch$df.residual

      lrt_b <- stats::anova(m_nobatch, m_bin, test = "Chisq")
      p_batch <- NA_real_
      pcol <- intersect(colnames(lrt_b), c("Pr(>Chi)", "Pr(>Chisq)"))
      if (length(pcol) > 0) p_batch <- unname(lrt_b[[pcol[1]]][2])

      ratio <- overdisp_bin / overdisp_nobatch

      if (is.finite(overdisp_nobatch) && is.finite(overdisp_bin) && is.finite(ratio) &&
          (overdisp_nobatch > overdisp_cut) &&
          (ratio <= batch_revert_ratio) &&
          (!is.na(p_batch) && p_batch < batch_revert_p) &&
          (overdisp_bin <= batch_revert_overdisp_max)) {
        tidy_bin$model_used <- "binomial_batch_explains"
        return(tidy_bin)
      }
    }

    # AUTO: if not meaningfully overdispersed, stick with binomial
    if (glm_family == "auto" && is.finite(overdisp_bin) && overdisp_bin <= overdisp_cut) {
      return(tidy_bin)
    }

    # From here: we want beta-binomial (explicit or auto when overdispersed)
    if (!requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)) {
      if (glm_family == "auto") return(fit_quasi_row("quasi_fallback"))
      stop("glm_family='betabinomial' requires 'glmmTMB'. Install it with install.packages('glmmTMB').")
    }

    bb_full <- fit_bb_robust(form_full, df_sub)
    m_full  <- bb_full$fit
    d_full  <- bb_full$diag

    # If beta cannot be fit, AUTO falls back to quasi; explicit beta returns NAs
    if (is.null(m_full)) {
      if (glm_family == "auto") {
        out <- fit_quasi_row("quasi_fallback")
        out$bb_conv   <- d_full$conv
        out$bb_pdHess <- d_full$pdHess
        out$bb_warn   <- d_full$warn
        return(out)
      }
      return(dplyr::tibble(
        term = pop_term, estimate = NA_real_, std.error = NA_real_,
        statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
        dispersion = NA_real_, overdisp = overdisp_bin,
        model_used = "betabinomial_failed",
        bb_conv = d_full$conv, bb_pdHess = d_full$pdHess, bb_warn = d_full$warn
      ))
    }

    # ============================================================
    # WALD inference for beta-binomial (matches binomial reporting)
    # ============================================================
    co <- summary(m_full)$coefficients$cond
    co_pop <- co[rownames(co) == pop_term, , drop = FALSE]

    est <- if (nrow(co_pop) == 1) unname(co_pop[1, "Estimate"]) else NA_real_
    se  <- if (nrow(co_pop) == 1) unname(co_pop[1, "Std. Error"]) else NA_real_
    z   <- if (nrow(co_pop) == 1 && "z value" %in% colnames(co_pop)) unname(co_pop[1, "z value"]) else NA_real_
    p_w <- if (nrow(co_pop) == 1 && "Pr(>|z|)" %in% colnames(co_pop)) unname(co_pop[1, "Pr(>|z|)"]) else NA_real_

    bb_sigma <- tryCatch(unname(stats::sigma(m_full)), error = function(e) NA_real_)

    out <- dplyr::tibble(
      term       = pop_term,
      estimate   = est,
      std.error  = se,
      statistic  = z,
      p.value    = p_w,
      dispersion = bb_sigma,
      overdisp   = overdisp_bin,
      model_used = "betabinomial",
      bb_conv    = d_full$conv,
      bb_pdHess  = d_full$pdHess,
      bb_warn    = d_full$warn
    )

    # Some fits can return NA Wald SE/p even if pdHess TRUE; AUTO falls back to quasi.
    if (glm_family == "auto" && (!is.finite(out$std.error) || !is.finite(out$p.value))) {
      qout <- fit_quasi_row("quasi_fallback")
      qout$bb_conv   <- d_full$conv
      qout$bb_pdHess <- d_full$pdHess
      qout$bb_warn   <- d_full$warn
      return(qout)
    }

    out
  }

  glm_effects <- props_by_sample %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.__group) %>%
    tidyr::nest() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(tidy = purrr::map(data, fit_and_tidy_one)) %>%
    dplyr::select(.__group, tidy) %>%
    tidyr::unnest(tidy) %>%
    {
      if (!"bb_conv" %in% names(.)) {
        .$bb_conv   <- NA_integer_
        .$bb_pdHess <- NA
        .$bb_warn   <- NA_character_
      }
      if (!"model_used" %in% names(.)) {
        .$model_used <- NA_character_
      }
      .
    } %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      odds_ratio = exp(estimate),
      p_adj = stats::p.adjust(p.value, "fdr"),
      sig = ifelse(p_adj < fdr_cutoff, paste0("FDR < ", fdr_cutoff), "NS")
    ) %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      group = as.character(.__group),
      term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value,
      dispersion, overdisp,
      p_adj, odds_ratio, sig,
      model_used,
      bb_conv, bb_pdHess, bb_warn
    ) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(p.value)

  # ============================================================
  # 4) Plot: bars + error bars + optional sample points
  # ============================================================
  ymult <- if (plot_percent) 100 else 1
  ylab  <- if (plot_percent) "Percentage composition" else "Proportion composition"

  p <- ggplot(cellprops, aes(fill = Var2, y = Freq * ymult, x = Var1)) +
    geom_bar(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), stat = "identity") +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = "Cell type", y = ylab, fill = "population") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkseagreen3", "palevioletred"))

  if (bar_error != "none") {
    p <- p +
      geom_errorbar(
        data = bar_df,
        aes(
          x = Var1,
          ymin = (mean_prop - if (bar_error == "sem") se_prop else sd_prop) * ymult,
          ymax = (mean_prop + if (bar_error == "sem") se_prop else sd_prop) * ymult,
          group = Var2
        ),
        inherit.aes = FALSE,
        color = "black",
        linewidth = 0.4,
        width = 0.25,
        position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)
      )
  }

  if (isTRUE(overlay_points)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_point(
        data = props_by_sample %>%
          dplyr::mutate(
            Var1 = factor(as.character(.__group), levels = keep_levels),
            Var2 = factor(as.character(.data[[pop_col]]), levels = pop_levels)
          ),
        aes(x = Var1, y = prop * ymult, fill = Var2),
        inherit.aes = FALSE,
        shape = 21,
        color = "black",
        size = 2,
        alpha = 0.8,
        position = position_jitterdodge(
          jitter.width = point_jitter,
          dodge.width  = 0.9
        )
      )
  }

  list(
    plot_bar = p,
    glm_effects = glm_effects,
    props_by_sample = props_by_sample,
    cellprops = cellprops,
    bar_df = bar_df,
    qc_sumprop = qc_sumprop,
    glm_family = glm_family,
    overdisp_cut = overdisp_cut
  )
}
```

### Pseudobulk DEGs 
#### Annotation - DEGs across cell types
```{r}
deseq2_pb_annotation <- function(
  cts,
  coldata,
  target_celltype,
  ref_celltypes = NULL,
  fdr_explore = 0.20,
  min_total_count = 10,
  min_samples = 2
) {

  stopifnot(is.matrix(cts) || inherits(cts, "dgCMatrix"))
  stopifnot(all(c("col_id","sample","Population","CellType") %in% colnames(coldata)))

  # clean coldata
  coldata <- as.data.frame(coldata, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  coldata$col_id     <- as.character(coldata$col_id)
  coldata$sample     <- as.character(coldata$sample)
  coldata$Population <- as.character(coldata$Population)
  coldata$CellType   <- as.character(coldata$CellType)

  # USE BOTH POPULATIONS for annotation (no subsetting)
  cd <- coldata
  if (nrow(cd) == 0) stop("coldata is empty after cleaning.")

  # optionally restrict which “other” celltypes are allowed
  if (!is.null(ref_celltypes)) {
    keep_cts <- unique(c(ref_celltypes, target_celltype))
    cd <- cd[cd$CellType %in% keep_cts, , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(cd) == 0) stop("After ref_celltypes filtering, nothing left.")
  }

  # need at least some target samples
  if (!any(cd$CellType == target_celltype)) {
    stop("No pseudobulk columns for target celltype: ", target_celltype)
  }

  # align counts to cd
  stopifnot(all(cd$col_id %in% colnames(cts)))
  cts2 <- cts[, cd$col_id, drop = FALSE]

  # define target vs other
  cd$is_target <- ifelse(cd$CellType == target_celltype, "target", "other")
  cd$is_target <- factor(cd$is_target, levels = c("other","target"))

  # Prefilter genes: expressed in at least min_samples pseudobulk columns at >= min_total_count
  keep <- Matrix::rowSums(cts2 >= min_total_count) >= min_samples
  cts2 <- cts2[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(cts2) == 0) stop("All genes filtered out; relax thresholds.")

  # DESeq2 colData must match column order
  cd2 <- cd[match(colnames(cts2), cd$col_id), , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(cts2), cd2$col_id))
  rownames(cd2) <- cd2$col_id

  # IMPORTANT: sample as a blocking factor (paired within sample)
  cd2$sample    <- factor(cd2$sample)
  cd2$is_target <- factor(cd2$is_target, levels = c("other","target"))

  dds <- DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = round(cts2),
    colData   = cd2,
    design    = ~ sample + is_target
  )

  # sanity: need both target and other
  if (length(unique(cd2$is_target)) < 2) {
    stop("Need both target and other columns after filtering.")
  }

  dds <- DESeq2::DESeq(dds)

  # results for target vs other
  res <- DESeq2::results(
    dds,
    contrast = c("is_target","target","other"),
    alpha = fdr_explore
  ) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("gene")

  res_all <- res |>
    dplyr::arrange(padj, dplyr::desc(baseMean))

  res_sig <- res_all |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(padj), padj < fdr_explore)

  list(
    dds             = dds,
    res_sig         = res_sig,
    res_all         = res_all,
    target_celltype = target_celltype,
    fdr_explore     = fdr_explore
  )
}
```

##### Export single cell type significant DEGs to csv
```{r}
format_and_write_annotation_csv <- function(
  res_df,
  neuro_cluster_label,          # e.g. "e2_tectum"
  padj_cut = 0.05,
  lfc_abs_min = 0,
  top_n = 100,
  drop_LOC = TRUE,
  loc_regex = "^LOC",
  extra_drop_regex = NULL
) {

  stopifnot(all(c("gene","padj","baseMean") %in% colnames(res_df)))

  df <- res_df

  # Optional filtering of LOC / unwanted symbols
  if (drop_LOC) {
    df <- df %>% filter(!grepl(loc_regex, gene))
  }
  if (!is.null(extra_drop_regex)) {
    df <- df %>% filter(!grepl(extra_drop_regex, gene))
  }

  # Keep significant genes
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(padj), padj <= padj_cut)

  # Determine which LFC column to use
  lfc_col <- if ("log2FoldChange_shrunk" %in% colnames(df)) {
    "log2FoldChange_shrunk"
  } else if ("log2FoldChange" %in% colnames(df)) {
    "log2FoldChange"
  } else {
    stop("res_df must contain log2FoldChange or log2FoldChange_shrunk")
  }

  # Keep only TARGET-ENRICHED genes
  df <- df %>% filter(.data[[lfc_col]] > 0)

  # Optional LFC threshold
  if (lfc_abs_min > 0) {
    df <- df %>% filter(abs(.data[[lfc_col]]) >= lfc_abs_min)
  }

  # Add direction column (useful for sanity checks)
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(direction = "Up in target")

  # Rank by: significance → specificity → expression
  df_out <- df %>%
    arrange(padj, desc(abs(.data[[lfc_col]])), desc(baseMean)) %>%
    slice_head(n = top_n)

  # Column order (clean CSV)
  preferred <- c("gene","baseMean",lfc_col,"padj","pvalue","stat","lfcSE","direction")
  keep_cols <- c(preferred, setdiff(colnames(df_out), preferred))
  df_out <- df_out %>% select(any_of(keep_cols))

  # Write directly to WORKING DIRECTORY
  fname <- paste0(neuro_cluster_label, ".csv")
  readr::write_csv(df_out, fname)

  message("Wrote annotation DEG CSV to: ", normalizePath(fname))

  return(df_out)
}
```

##### Export all cell type markers with log2fold change cutoff
```{r}
run_all_celltype_deg_exports <- function(
  cts,
  coldata,
  padj_cut = 0.05,
  lfc_min = 1,
  positive_only = TRUE,
  out_csv = "AllCellTypes_DEGs_filtered.csv",
  verbose = TRUE
) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(dplyr)
    library(readr)
  })

  stopifnot(is.matrix(cts) || inherits(cts, "dgCMatrix"))
  stopifnot(all(c("col_id","sample","Population","CellType") %in% colnames(coldata)))

  cd <- as.data.frame(coldata, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  celltypes <- sort(unique(cd$CellType))
  celltypes <- celltypes[!is.na(celltypes) & celltypes != ""]

  if (length(celltypes) == 0) stop("No celltypes found in coldata.")

  results_list <- vector("list", length(celltypes))
  names(results_list) <- celltypes

  failures <- list()

  for (ct in celltypes) {
    if (isTRUE(verbose)) message("Running DESeq2 for: ", ct)

    out <- try(
      deseq2_pb_annotation(
        cts = cts,
        coldata = cd,
        target_celltype = ct
      ),
      silent = TRUE
    )

    if (inherits(out, "try-error")) {
      failures[[ct]] <- as.character(out)
      next
    }

    df <- out$res_all %>%
      mutate(celltype = ct) %>%
      select(celltype, gene, padj, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, pvalue, baseMean) %>%
      filter(!is.na(padj), padj <= padj_cut) %>%
      filter(!is.na(log2FoldChange))

    if (positive_only) {
      df <- df %>%
        filter(log2FoldChange >= lfc_min)
    } else {
      df <- df %>%
        filter(abs(log2FoldChange) >= lfc_min)
    }

    df <- df %>%
      arrange(celltype, desc(log2FoldChange), padj, desc(baseMean))

    results_list[[ct]] <- df
  }

  combined_results <- bind_rows(results_list)

  readr::write_csv(combined_results, out_csv)

  if (isTRUE(verbose)) {
    message("Wrote filtered DEG file: ", normalizePath(out_csv))
    if (length(failures) > 0) {
      message("Some cell types failed. Check returned $failures.")
    }
  }

  return(list(
    degs = combined_results,
    failures = failures
  ))
}
```

#### Population - subset to cell type for surface vs cave
```{r}
deseq2_pb_celltype <- function(cts, coldata, celltype,
                               fdr_explore = 0.20,
                               min_total_count = 10,
                               min_samples = 2,
                               shrink_type = c("apeglm", "ashr", "normal")) {

  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(Matrix)
    library(DESeq2)
    library(dplyr)
    library(tibble)
  })

  shrink_type <- match.arg(shrink_type)

  stopifnot(is.matrix(cts) || inherits(cts, "dgCMatrix"))
  stopifnot(all(c("col_id","sample","Population","CellType") %in% colnames(coldata)))

  # Coerce to plain data.frame to avoid Rle/list columns breaking dplyr verbs
  coldata <- as.data.frame(coldata, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  coldata$col_id     <- as.character(coldata$col_id)
  coldata$sample     <- as.character(coldata$sample)
  coldata$Population <- as.character(coldata$Population)
  coldata$CellType   <- as.character(coldata$CellType)

  # Align count columns
  stopifnot(all(coldata$col_id %in% colnames(cts)))
  cts <- cts[, coldata$col_id, drop = FALSE]

  # Subset to the requested cell type (already pseudobulked columns)
  cd_ct <- coldata[coldata$CellType == celltype, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(cd_ct) == 0) stop("No pseudobulk samples for celltype: ", celltype)

  cts_ct <- cts[, cd_ct$col_id, drop = FALSE]

  # Prefilter genes
  keep <- Matrix::rowSums(cts_ct >= min_total_count) >= min_samples
  cts_ct <- cts_ct[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(cts_ct) == 0) stop("All genes filtered out; relax thresholds.")

  # Build DESeq2 colData and reorder to match columns
  cd_ct2 <- unique(cd_ct[, c("col_id", "sample", "Population")])
  cd_ct2 <- cd_ct2[match(colnames(cts_ct), cd_ct2$col_id), , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(cts_ct), cd_ct2$col_id))
  rownames(cd_ct2) <- cd_ct2$col_id

  # DESeq2
  dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = round(cts_ct),
    colData   = cd_ct2,
    design    = ~ Population
  )

  dds$Population <- factor(dds$Population)
  if (!("surface" %in% levels(dds$Population))) {
    stop("Population must include 'surface'. Found: ", paste(levels(dds$Population), collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (length(levels(dds$Population)) != 2) {
    stop("This function assumes exactly 2 Population levels. Found: ", paste(levels(dds$Population), collapse = ", "))
  }

  dds$Population <- relevel(dds$Population, ref = "surface")
  dds <- DESeq(dds)

  alt <- setdiff(levels(dds$Population), "surface")[1]
  coef_name <- paste0("Population_", make.names(alt), "_vs_surface")
  if (!coef_name %in% resultsNames(dds)) {
    coef_name <- resultsNames(dds)[grepl("^Population_", resultsNames(dds))][1]
  }

  res <- results(dds, name = coef_name, alpha = fdr_explore) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("gene")

  res_shr <- tryCatch({
    shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = coef_name, type = shrink_type)
    as.data.frame(shr) |> tibble::rownames_to_column("gene")
  }, error = function(e) {
    shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = coef_name, type = "normal")
    as.data.frame(shr) |> tibble::rownames_to_column("gene")
  })

  res_merged <- res |>
    dplyr::left_join(
      res_shr |> dplyr::select(gene, log2FoldChange) |> dplyr::rename(log2FoldChange_shrunk = log2FoldChange),
      by = "gene"
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(padj, dplyr::desc(abs(log2FoldChange_shrunk)))

  res_celltype <- res_merged |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(padj), padj < fdr_explore)

  list(
    dds          = dds,
    res_celltype = res_celltype,
    res_all      = res_merged,
    celltype     = celltype,
    coef_name    = coef_name,
    fdr_explore  = fdr_explore
  )
}
```
### Plotting
```{r}
mini_axis_umap <- function(
  seurat_obj,
  reduction = "umap",
  group.by = NULL,
  split.by = NULL,
  label = TRUE,
  shuffle = TRUE,
  alpha = 0.8,
  pt.size = 0.5,
  axis_frac = 0.08,
  pad_frac  = 0.03,
  arrow_mm  = 2,
  linewidth = 0.5,
  add_labels = TRUE,
  label_x = "UMAP 1",
  label_y = "UMAP 2",
  label_size = 3,
  margin_mm = 5.5,
  seed = NULL
) {
  stopifnot(inherits(seurat_obj, "Seurat"))

  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)

  # 1) Base DimPlot
  p <- DimPlot(
    seurat_obj,
    reduction = reduction,
    group.by = group.by,
    split.by = split.by,
    label = label,
    shuffle = shuffle,
    alpha = alpha,
    pt.size = pt.size
  ) + NoLegend()

  # 2) Remove axes completely
  p_clean <- p +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(margin_mm, margin_mm, margin_mm, margin_mm, unit = "mm")) +
    NoLegend()

  # 3) Compute panel ranges
  gb <- ggplot_build(p_clean)
  pp <- gb$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  x_rng <- pp$x.range
  y_rng <- pp$y.range

  x_span <- diff(x_rng)
  y_span <- diff(y_rng)

  # Bottom-left corner position (with padding)
  x0 <- x_rng[1] + pad_frac * x_span
  y0 <- y_rng[1] + pad_frac * y_span

  # Mini-axis lengths
  dx <- axis_frac * x_span
  dy <- axis_frac * y_span

  # 4) Add mini-axes + optional labels
  p_final <- p_clean +
    annotate(
      "segment",
      x = x0, xend = x0 + dx,
      y = y0, yend = y0,
      linewidth = linewidth,
      arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(arrow_mm, "mm"))
    ) +
    annotate(
      "segment",
      x = x0, xend = x0,
      y = y0, yend = y0 + dy,
      linewidth = linewidth,
      arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(arrow_mm, "mm"))
    )

  if (isTRUE(add_labels)) {
    p_final <- p_final +
      annotate(
        "text",
        x = x0 + dx, y = y0 - 0.01 * y_span,
        label = label_x, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = label_size
      ) +
      annotate(
        "text",
        x = x0 - 0.01 * x_span, y = y0 + dy,
        label = label_y, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 90, size = label_size
      )
  }

  return(p_final)
}
```

## Annotate brain clusters
### b1: Meningeal fibroblasts

Cluster b1: Meningeal fibroblasts

One-line identity: Collagen-rich cranial mesenchyme–derived meningeal fibroblasts, most consistent with leptomeningeal/pial–arachnoid stromal cells that specialize in extracellular matrix production, matrix remodeling, and local morphogen signaling rather than neural, vascular, or immune identity. This interpretation is supported by the combination of strong fibrillar/ECM collagen expression, a pdgfra+ fibroblast program, cranial mesenchyme transcription factors, and stromal signaling genes that fit zebrafish fibroblast and meningeal-associated support populations (Banerjee et al., 2022; Dee et al., 2013; Eberhart et al., 2006; Lendahl et al., 2022; Psutkova et al., 2025; Rajan et al., 2020).  
 
Key evidence
• Definitive fibroblast / ECM-producing stromal program:
col12a1a, col12a1b, col11a1b, col11a2, col5a1, col5a2a, col6a1, col6a2, col1a1b, col22a1, col23a1a, col27a1a, hapln1a, tncb, tnca, vcana, fbn1, fbn2b, mfap2, tgfbi, mmp14a, adamts17, adamts18
→ The dominant signal is a matrix-secreting connective-tissue phenotype rather than glial or endothelial identity. In zebrafish, fibroblast populations are defined by strong collagen/ECM expression, and recent single-cell work also emphasizes broad fibroblast heterogeneity with distinct matrix-producing subtypes. The prominence of multiple fibrillar collagens, proteoglycan-associated ECM genes, and matrix-remodeling enzymes strongly supports annotation as fibroblasts.  

• pdgfra mesenchymal fibroblast identity:
pdgfra, itga11a, cdh11, myh10, plpp3, scara5
→ pdgfra is one of the strongest anchors for this annotation. Zebrafish studies identify pdgfra-expressing cells as fibroblast as well as fibroblast precursors that migrate and diversify into fibroblast subtypes. The additional presence of itga11a and cdh11 further supports a mesenchymal fibroblast interpretation rather than meningeal endothelium or mural cells.  

• Cranial mesenchyme / meningeal connective-tissue patterning program:
alx4a, meis1a, gli2b, glis2a, nfatc4, runx2b, twist-like mesenchymal context from your broader marker set
→ This cluster carries a cranial mesenchyme-like regulatory profile. In zebrafish, twist1 is expressed in craniofacial/head mesenchyme and alx4a is expressed in craniofacial/frontonasal mesenchyme and connective-tissue lineages. This makes the DEG combination more consistent with cranial meningeal / head-associated fibroblastic mesenchyme than with peripheral connective tissue.  
• Stromal signaling and morphogen-organizing niche features:
wnt5a, wnt5b, rspo2, ntn1a, boc, cdon, ptch1, tgfbi
→ These genes suggest that the cells are not merely structural ECM producers; they likely contribute to a local signaling niche. Fibroblast populations are functionally diverse and can act as signaling-organizing stromal cells, while leptomeningeal support populations in zebrafish also participate in local brain-surface vascular and stromal organization. 

**Decision rule:**

The combined presence of a strong collagen- and proteoglycan-rich ECM program, pdgfra-positive fibroblast identity, cranial mesenchymal transcription factors, and stromal morphogen/signaling genes supports annotation as meningeal fibroblasts. The profile is more consistent with brain-surface connective tissue of meningeal origin than with mural cells, endothelial cells, glia, or neural crest–derived neurons.  

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from mural/perivascular cells by its much stronger fibrillar collagen and matrix-remodeling profile, from cartilage/osteogenic mesenchyme by the lack of a dominant chondrocyte or osteoblast program, and from CNS glia by the absence of canonical glial transport/homeostasis markers. What stands out most is a pdgfra cranial fibroblast identity coupled to heavy ECM deposition, which is exactly the kind of profile expected for meningeal fibroblasts associated with pia/arachnoid connective tissue. 


```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(
  
    # Fibroblast / ECM-producing stromal program
    "col12a1a", "col12a1b", "col11a1b", "col11a2",
    "col5a1", "col5a2a", "col6a1", "col6a2",
    "col1a1b", "col22a1", "col23a1a", "col27a1a",
    "hapln1a", "tncb", "tnca", "vcana", "fbn1", "fbn2b",
    "mfap2", "tgfbi", "mmp14a", "adamts17", "adamts18",

    # pdgfra mesenchymal fibroblast identity
    "pdgfra", "itga11a", "cdh11", "myh10", "plpp3", "scara5",

    # Cranial mesenchyme / meningeal patterning
    "alx4a", "meis1a", "gli2b", "glis2a", "nfatc4", "runx2b",

    # Stromal signaling / morphogen niche
    "wnt5a", "wnt5b", "rspo2", "ntn1a", "boc", "cdon", "ptch1"
    
  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```


### b2: BBB

**Cluster b2: Brain endothelium / BBB-like**

One-line identity: Arterial-leaning brain endothelial cells with a strong BBB-like barrier and transporter program, defined by a canonical endothelial/vascular core together with cldn5a- and slc2a1a-linked barrier features, brain-enriched solute transporters, and arterial Notch signaling, consistent with zebrafish cerebrovascular endothelium specialized for blood-brain barrier function rather than tip-like angiogenic, lymphatic, or fenestrated vascular states (Hasan et al., 2017; Hotz et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Quiñonez-Silvero et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2010).  
 

**Key evidence**

  • Definitive endothelial / cerebrovascular identity: pecam1b, cdh5, tie1, kdr, kdrl, flt1, ptprb, egfl7, esama, plxnd1, nrp1b, pcdh12
    → The combination of VE-cadherin/cdh5, PECAM, VEGFR/kdr-kdrl, Tie, ptprb, egfl7, and esama is a classic vascular endothelial program and
    zebrafish brain-vasculature work specifically places these genes within developing cerebrovascular endothelium rather than mural, meningeal,
    or glial populations.  
 
  • BBB-like barrier and junction program: cldn5a, cgnl1, jam2a, clic2, tmem204, rasip1, heg1
    → Cldn5a is required for proper BBB function, and BBB maturation studies also emphasize endothelial junctional specialization and
    suppression of non-barrier permeability mechanisms as key features of brain endothelial identity.  

  • Brain-endothelial transporter / metabolic specialization: slc2a1a, slc38a5b, slco4a1, slco1c1, slco2a1, slc7a5, slc7a3a, slc31a1, abcb4,
  abcc4, abcg2a, scarb2a, scarb2b
    → Slc2a1a/GLUT1 is a canonical BBB-associated transporter and the broader enrichment of nutrient, solute, and efflux transport systems fits
    a metabolically selective brain endothelial state. Abcb4 and BBB-associated ABC transport activity is also part of a specialized endothelial
    barrier program in zebrafish.  
 
  • Arterial-leaning endothelial specification: dll4, kdrl, kdr, flt1, klf2a, epas1a, erg, mef2aa, tbx3a, acvrl1, eng
    → This cluster is not just BBB-like; it is also arterial-biased. Endothelial Notch signaling studies directly link dll4/Notch to artery
    formation and restriction of angiogenic behavior. The accompanying flow/shear and endothelial TF module (klf2a, erg, epas1a, mef2aa)
    reinforces an arterial cerebrovascular identity rather than venous or lymphatic endothelium.  

**Decision rule:**

The combined presence of a definitive endothelial core, a strong cldn5a/slc2a1a BBB-like barrier and transporter program, and a dll4/arterial signaling axis supports annotation as brain endothelium / BBB-like, arterial-biased.  

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from more angiogenic endothelial states by its stronger barrier/junction and transporter specialization, from lymphatic endothelium by the lack of a convincing lymphatic marker set, and from fenestrated endothelium by its BBB-associated cldn5a and slc2a1a profile. 

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Definitive endothelial / cerebrovascular identity
    "pecam1b", "cdh5", "tie1", "kdr", "kdrl", "flt1",
    "ptprb", "egfl7", "esama", "plxnd1", "nrp1b", "pcdh12",

    # BBB-like barrier and junction program
    "cldn5a", "cgnl1", "jam2a", "clic2",
    "tmem204", "rasip1", "heg1",

    # Brain-endothelial transporter / metabolic specialization
    "slc2a1a", "slc38a5b", "slco4a1", "slco1c1",
    "slco2a1", "slc7a5", "slc7a3a", "slc31a1",
    "abcb4", "abcc4", "abcg2a", "scarb2a", "scarb2b",

    # Arterial-leaning endothelial specification
    "dll4", "klf2a", "epas1a", "erg",
    "mef2aa", "tbx3a", "acvrl1", "eng"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```


### b3: mLSCs

**Cluster b3: mLSCs (meningeal lymphatic supporting cells)**

One-line identity: Non-endothelial leptomeningeal support cells consistent with the zebrafish mLSC state described by He et al. 2024, defined by epd together with pro-lymphangiogenic support genes, basement-membrane / ECM components, metabolite and lipid transporters, and a meningeal mesenchymal transcriptional program, consistent with cells that wrap and support muLECs and adjacent meningeal blood vessels rather than forming lymphatic endothelium themselves (Grimm et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Jha et al., 2017; Le Guen et al., 2014; Uphoff et al., 2026).  
 
**Key evidence**

  • Definitive mLSC-support-cell identity: epd, ccbe1, vegfc, pdgfra, ramp2, lamc3, flvcr2b, apof, slc38a4, vcam1b
   → mLSCs described in He et al. 2024 are specifically epd-positive, form membranous leptomeningeal structures, and wrap most leptomeningeal
   blood vessels. 
 
  • Pro-lymphangiogenic support program rather than lymphatic endothelial identity: ccbe1, vegfc, ramp2, pdgfra, bmp7b, gas6, pros1
   → These genes fit a supportive niche for meningeal lymphatic cells, not a mature LEC identity. mLECs depend on the Vegfc–Vegfd–Ccbe1 pathway
   for development and act as upstream as the supportive meningeal cell type that helps drive muLEC development, maintenance, and regeneration. 
  
  • Basement membrane / meningeal ECM scaffold: nid1a, lamc3, col4a5, lama2, col18a1a, mmp14b, loxl1, emilin1b, vcam1b
   → This cluster is rich in extracellular-matrix and basement-membrane genes, which fits the structural role of mLSCs that act as
   membrane-forming leptomeningeal support cells. The strong laminin/collagen/nidogen/LOX signal argues that these are stromal wrapping cells
   building or maintaining the local meningeal matrix around vessels and muLECs.  
  
  • Metabolic / lipid / solute support module: flvcr2b, apof, slc38a4, slc20a2, slc7a2, slc7a8a, slc13a3, slc13a5a, abca1b, glula, glulb
   → mLSCs are transporter-rich and metabolically supportive, with multiple solute carriers plus lipid-handling genes such as apof and abca1b.  
 
  • Meningeal mesenchymal / stromal transcriptional program: foxp1a, foxp1b, alx4a, glis2a, gli1, zic2a, zic4
   → This TF module supports a specialized meningeal stromal identity layered onto the lymphatic-support phenotype.  

  • Distinguished from muLECs and blood endothelial cells:
   → lack of a canonical lymphatic endothelial core such as prox1a, lyve1b, flt4/vegfr3, and mrc1a, and lack of a blood endothelial core such as
   kdrl, cdh5, and pecam1 among DEGs.

**Decision rule:**

The combined presence of epd, a Vegfc/Ccbe1-linked lymphangiogenic support module, strong meningeal ECM/basement-membrane genes, abundant solute and lipid transporters, and absence of a defining endothelial identity supports annotation as mLSCs.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster lacks the canonical lymphatic endothelial program of muLECs as well as the core vascular endothelial signature of brain endothelium. Compared with more generic fibroblast-like meningeal stromal cells, it is specifically marked by the epd + pro-lymphangiogenic support profile defined as mLSCs in He et al. 2024.  

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # mLSC support-cell identity
    "epd", "ccbe1", "vegfc", "pdgfra", "ramp2",
    "lamc3", "flvcr2b", "apof", "slc38a4", "vcam1b",

    # Pro-lymphangiogenic support program
    "bmp7b", "gas6", "pros1",

    # Basement membrane / meningeal ECM scaffold
    "nid1a", "col4a5", "lama2", "col18a1a",
    "mmp14b", "loxl1", "emilin1b",

    # Metabolic / lipid / solute support module
    "slc20a2", "slc7a2", "slc7a8a",
    "slc13a3", "slc13a5a", "abca1b",
    "glula", "glulb",

    # Meningeal mesenchymal / stromal TF program
    "foxp1a", "foxp1b", "alx4a",
    "glis2a", "gli1", "zic2a", "zic4"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```


### b4: Mural cells

**Cluster b4: Mixed mural cells (pericyte + vascular smooth muscle continuum)**

One-line identity: Mixed mural cell population exhibiting both pericyte (pdgfrb/rgs5) and contractile smooth muscle (acta2/tagln/myh11a) programs, consistent with a pericyte–vSMC continuum (Ando et al., 2021; Colijn et al., 2024; Leonard et al., 2022; Ryu et al., 2022; Shih et al., 2021; Whitesell et al., 2019; Zi et al., 2024).
 
**Key evidence**

• Core mural-cell identity (shared perivascular lineage): pdgfrb, rgs5a, mcamb, cd248a, notch3
→ These genes define canonical vascular mural cells in zebrafish, marking cells that physically associate with and stabilize blood vessels. pdgfrb signaling is required for mural-cell recruitment, while rgs5 is a widely used pericyte/mural marker. The presence of notch3 further supports mural identity linked to vessel wall differentiation.

• Pericyte-associated program: pdgfrb, rgs5a, rgs12b, cd248a, mcam/mcamb, gpr4, ndufa4l2a, kcne4
→ These genes are classically enriched in pericytes, particularly capillary-associated mural cells involved in endothelial interaction, vessel stabilization, and signaling. This component indicates a clear pericyte-like identity within the cluster rather than purely smooth muscle cells.

• Contractile smooth muscle (vSMC-like) program: acta2, tagln, myh11a, mylkb, mylka, myl9b, tpm1, tpm4a,
tpm4b, cald1a, myocd, lmod1b
→ This is a robust actomyosin contractile machinery, characteristic of vascular smooth muscle cells. Genes such as acta2, tagln, and myh11a define differentiated vSMCs, while myocd and cald1a support smooth muscle specialization. This indicates that a substantial fraction of the cluster exhibits vSMC-like functional properties.

• Vascular tone and signaling machinery: gucy1a1, gucy1a2, ednraa, prkg1a, pde3a, pde5ab, s1pr2, adra1aa,
cacna1c
→ These genes mediate vasoreactivity, nitric oxide signaling, and contractile regulation, supporting a functional role in controlling vessel tone, which is characteristic of contractile mural cells (especially arteriolar vSMCs).

• Basement membrane / vessel wall ECM: col4a1, col4a2, col5a3a, col6a1, col6a2, col6a4a, lama4, lamb1b,
lamc1, lamc3, colec12, itga1
→ Mural cells contribute to and reside within the vascular basement membrane. This strong ECM signature supports structural integration within the vessel wall, distinguishing these cells from non-vascular fibroblasts.

• Developmental and lineage regulators: foxc1b, tbx2a, tbx2b, hey1, hey2, mef2cb, klf12a, notch1b, notch3
→ These transcription factors are associated with mural-cell differentiation and vascular development, including smooth muscle specification and Notch-dependent arterial programs. Their presence supports a continuum of mural differentiation states rather than a single fixed identity.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a pdgfrb/rgs5/notch3 mural-cell core together with a robust contractile smooth muscle module (acta2, tagln, myh11a, mylkb, cald1a, and myocd) supports annotation as mural cells. The clear co-expression of both pericyte-associated and vSMC-defining genes, without separation into distinct populations, supports interpretation as a mixed mural population spanning pericyte and smooth muscle states, rather than a single discrete subtype.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from more fibroblast-like perivascular stromal cells by its clear actomyosin contractile machinery, and from canonical capillary pericytes by its strong enrichment of vSMC markers such as acta2, tagln, myh11a, mylkb, cald1a, and myocd. At the same time, retention of pericyte markers (pdgfrb, rgs5a, cd248a) indicates that these cells do not represent a purely smooth muscle population. Instead, the dominant signal is a mural continuum state, capturing both pericyte and contractile smooth muscle features within a single cluster.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Core mural-cell identity
    "pdgfrb", "rgs5a", "mcamb", "cd248a", "notch3",

    # Pericyte-associated program
    "rgs12b", "gpr4", "ndufa4l2a", "kcne4",

    # Contractile smooth muscle (vSMC-like) program
    "acta2", "tagln", "myh11a", "mylkb", "mylka",
    "myl9b", "tpm1", "tpm4a", "tpm4b",
    "cald1a", "myocd", "lmod1b",

    # Vascular tone and signaling machinery
    "gucy1a1", "gucy1a2", "ednraa",
    "prkg1a", "pde3a", "pde5ab",
    "s1pr2", "adra1aa", "cacna1c",

    # Basement membrane / vessel wall ECM
    "col4a1", "col4a2", "col5a3a",
    "col6a1", "col6a2", "col6a4a",
    "lama4", "lamb1b", "lamc1", "lamc3",
    "colec12", "itga1",

    # Developmental and lineage regulators
    "foxc1b", "tbx2a", "tbx2b",
    "hey1", "hey2", "mef2cb",
    "klf12a", "notch1b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```


### b5: pineal epithelial cells

**Cluster b5: Pineal epithelial cells**

One-line identity: Multiciliated pineal support cells, defined by a strong foxj1-driven motile cilia program, epithelial transport/ion-handling machinery, and pineal-lineage transcription factors, together with expression of visual-cycle / opsin-like genes (rgra, rrh) but absence of a canonical phototransduction cascade, consistent with the non-photoreceptor pineal support cell population described in zebrafish (D’Gama et al., 2021; Elazary et al., 2023; W. H. Li et al., 2015; Mano et al., 2019; Olstad et al., 2019).
 
**Key evidence**

• Pineal / epithalamic lineage identity: otx2b, lmx1ba, lmx1bb, barhl2, zic2a, zic4, otx1
→ These transcription factors support a pineal/epithalamic epithelial lineage rather than generic ventricular epithelium. Otx/Lmx programs are central to zebrafish pineal specification and maintenance, anchoring this cluster to pineal tissue rather than broadly distributed ependyma.

• Pineal glial / neuroepithelial support markers: fabp7a, atp1a1b
→ Co-expression of fabp7a (lipid/metabolic support; canonical radial glial/neuroepithelial marker) and atp1a1b (ion transport and homeostasis) is consistent with non-photoreceptor pineal support cells with glial/neuroepithelial characteristics, as described in zebrafish pineal support cell populations (Elazary et al., 2023).

• Multiciliated epithelial / ependymal-like program: foxj1a, foxj1b, dnah5, dnah9, dnah12, dnah7, dnaaf11,
cfap45, cfap58, cfap221, tekt1, fsip1, intu
→ A robust motile cilia gene network characteristic of Foxj1-dependent multiciliated epithelial cells. In zebrafish, this program defines ventricular and specialized epithelial cell types, including ciliated cells associated with brain cavities and sensory interfaces.

• Transport / ion-handling support physiology: slc23a2, slc12a4, slc4a5b, slc4a2a, slc4a10b, slc6a4a,
slc7a1a, slc29a1a, slc47a1, slco1e1, atp2b2, atp1b3b, trpm3, wnk4b
→ Strong enrichment for solute transporters and ion regulators, consistent with epithelial support functions, including regulation of extracellular environment and metabolite exchange—hallmarks of non-neuronal pineal support cells.

• Visual-cycle / opsin-like support features (non-photoreceptor): rgra, rrh, lratd2b
→ Expression of RGR/RRH-type opsin-like genes and retinoid-associated factors without a full phototransduction cascade. Zebrafish pineal support/glial cells have been shown to express visual-cycle genes required for photoreceptor maintenance while remaining molecularly distinct from photoreceptors (Elazary et al., 2023).

• Absence of canonical photoreceptor program: (no pde6c, gngt1, prph2b, impg1b, arrestins)
→ The lack of core phototransduction machinery excludes pineal photoreceptor identity, despite the presence of opsin-like genes.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a pineal-lineage transcriptional program (otx2/lmx/zic factors) together with a dominant foxj1-driven multiciliated epithelial signature, strong transport/ion-handling physiology, and the presence of visual-cycle/opsin-like genes (rgra, rrh) without a phototransduction cascade supports annotation as pineal support cells, specifically a multiciliated, non-photoreceptor epithelial/glial population associated with the pineal organ.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from pineal photoreceptors by the absence of a full phototransduction program and instead exhibits a strong multiciliated epithelial and support-cell physiology. It is distinguished from generic ventricular ependymal cells by its retention of pineal/epithalamic transcription factors (otx2b, lmx1ba/lmx1bb, barhl2) and visual-cycle gene expression, which align with recently described pineal-specific support/glial cells. The dominant signal is therefore pineal-associated multiciliated support cells, not generic ependyma and not photoreceptors.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Pineal / epithalamic lineage identity
    "otx2b", "lmx1ba", "lmx1bb", "barhl2",
    "zic2a", "zic4", "otx1",

    # Pineal glial / neuroepithelial support markers
    "fabp7a", "atp1a1b",

    # Multiciliated epithelial / ependymal-like program
    "foxj1a", "foxj1b", "dnah5", "dnah9",
    "dnah12", "dnah7", "dnaaf11",
    "cfap45", "cfap58", "cfap221",
    "tekt1", "fsip1", "intu",

    # Transport / ion-handling support physiology
    "slc23a2", "slc12a4", "slc4a5b",
    "slc4a2a", "slc4a10b", "slc6a4a",
    "slc7a1a", "slc29a1a", "slc47a1",
    "slco1e1", "atp2b2", "atp1b3b",
    "trpm3", "wnk4b",

    # Visual-cycle / opsin-like support features
    "rgra", "rrh", "lratd2b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### b6: Choroid plexus epithelium

Cluster b6: Choroid plexus epithelium

One-line identity: Choroid plexus epithelial cells — specialized ventricular epithelial cells forming the blood–CSF barrier, defined by a polarized epithelial junction program together with strong transporter-driven CSF secretion and lipid/metabolic processing characteristic of zebrafish choroid plexus (Alvers et al., 2014; Henson et al., 2014; Heppert et al., 2022; Jeong et al., 2024; Parab et al., 2021).
.  
Key evidence

• Definitive choroid plexus epithelial / blood–CSF barrier identity:
cldn15la, cdh17, cdhr2,  mpzl3, patj, itga3a, vegfaa/b
→ The choroid plexus forms as a ventricular epithelial sheet with tight junctions and apical–basal polarity that constitute the blood–CSF barrier. The presence of epithelial adhesion and junction components (claudins, cadherins, polarity scaffolds) directly supports a choroid plexus epithelial identity rather than endothelial, mesenchymal, or generic ependymal cells.

• CSF secretion / transporter-rich epithelial physiology:
slc5a1, slc43a2b, slc4a4a, slc26a6, slc23a1, slco1e1, abcc4, slc2a2, slc15a1b
→ Choroid plexus epithelial cells are defined by dense expression of solute carriers and transporters that mediate controlled exchange between blood and CSF. 

• Lipid transport and apolipoprotein-associated program:
apoba, apobb.1, cd36, fabp2, slc27a4, slc27a2a, dgat1a, dgat1b, lpcat3, plin3, npc1
→ The strong lipid uptake, intracellular trafficking, and lipoprotein-related machinery supports a metabolically active secretory epithelium, consistent with choroid plexus roles in CSF composition and molecular transport, rather than passive barrier tissue.

• Detoxification and metabolic filtering functions:
ugt2a5, ces2b, cyp-related genes, gpx4a, acox1, acox3, hsd17b4, glud1a, glud1b, pck1, fbp1b
→ Choroid plexus epithelium functions as a biochemical filter at the blood–CSF interface, and this cluster shows a strong enrichment for xenobiotic metabolism, lipid oxidation, and redox regulation, supporting that specialized barrier/secretory role.

• Epithelial transcriptional regulators consistent with secretory barrier identity:
hnf4a, hnf4b, hnf4g, nr1h4, gata6, creb3l3b
→ These transcription factors support a highly specialized absorptive/secretory epithelial state, reinforcing that this cluster is not neuronal or glial, but a functionally specialized epithelial barrier tissue, consistent with choroid plexus differentiation and function.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a ventricular epithelial barrier program, dense transporter expression consistent with CSF secretion, strong lipid/apolipoprotein handling, and a secretory metabolic-detoxification signature supports annotation as choroid plexus epithelium.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from generic ependymal cells by its much stronger transporter, lipid-handling, and detoxification programs, and from vascular barrier cells by its epithelial cadherin/junction profile and lack of a canonical endothelial identity. The dominant signal is secretory choroid plexus epithelium forming the blood–CSF barrier, not ordinary ventricular lining cells.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Choroid plexus epithelial / blood–CSF barrier identity
    "cldn15la", "cdh17", "cdhr2", 
    "mpzl3", "patj", "itga3a", "vegfaa", "vegfab",

    # CSF secretion / transporter-rich epithelial physiology
    "slc5a1", "slc43a2b", "slc4a4a",
    "slc26a6", "slc23a1", "slco1e1",
    "abcc4", "slc2a2", "slc15a1b",

    # Lipid transport and apolipoprotein-associated program
    "apoba", "apobb.1", "cd36", "fabp2",
    "slc27a4", "slc27a2a", "dgat1a", "dgat1b",
    "lpcat3", "plin3", "npc1",

    # Detoxification and metabolic filtering functions
    "ugt2a5", "ces2b", "gpx4a",
    "acox1", "acox3", "hsd17b4",
    "glud1a", "glud1b", "pck1", "fbp1b",

    # Epithelial transcriptional regulators
    "hnf4a", "hnf4b", "hnf4g",
    "nr1h4", "gata6", "creb3l3b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### b7: Pineal photoreceptors

**Cluster b7: Pineal photoreceptors**

One-line identity: Melatonin-producing, opsin-expressing pineal photoreceptor cells with a strong zebrafish pineal photoreceptor program, including direct photosensitivity, phototransduction machinery, retinoid-handling genes, and pineal-specifying transcription factors, rather than retinal carryover (Davies et al., 2015; Lagman et al., 2015; Mano et al., 2019; Sapède et al., 2020; Seritrakul & Gross, 2019; Vitorino et al., 2009).  
 
**Key evidence**

• Pineal neuroendocrine / melatonin-output identity: asmt, nfil3-6, bhlhe40, per2, npas2, tefa, hlfa
→ This cluster carries a strong pineal circadian-neuroendocrine program. In zebrafish, the pineal gland is a melatonin-producing, directly photoreceptive circadian organ and asmt is a strong pineal anchor in zebrafish brain tissue. 

• Direct pineal photosensitivity / opsin repertoire: opn4b, opn4xa, opn5, opn7b, opn8b, opn9
→ The pineal is a well-established photosensitive organ in zebrafish, and transcriptomic work on zebrafish opsins showed that the pineal complex expresses a large opsin repertoire. 

• Photoreceptor structural and phototransduction machinery: prom1b, rdh8a, rpe65a, rgrb, rgra, slc24a4a,
trpm1b, myo7ab
→ Zebrafish pineal photoreceptors are known to share core molecular and functional features with retinal photoreceptors. 

• Retinoid-handling / visual-cycle-like program: rpe65a, rdh5, rdh8a, stra6, rgra, rgrb, rbp5, rbp4l
→ This cluster has a retinoid-processing signature that is highly compatible with the zebrafish pineal. Recent zebrafish work showed that the pineal contains cells expressing visual-cycle genes and that these cells are required for pineal photoreceptor maintenance; additional zebrafish pineal studies explicitly note expression of visual-cycle genes such as rpe65a and rgra in the pineal gland.  

• Pineal transcription factor program: otx5, lhx2b, pax7a, pax7b, bsx
→ Otx5 is a core regulator of pineal photoreceptor/circadian gene expression, and bsx + otx5 together specify pineal photoreceptive identity. 

• Not retinal carryover: absence of vsx2, gnat1, pde6a, pde6b, nr2e3, atoh7, pou4f2 
→ These genes are canonical zebrafish retinal-lineage or retinal photoreceptor/RGC markers, so their absence makes a retinal carryover explanation much less likely.  

**Decision rule:**

The combined presence of a strong pineal melatonin/circadian module (asmt, nfil3-6, bhlhe40, and per2), a broad pineal opsin repertoire (opn4b, opn4xa, opn5, opn7b, opn8b, and opn9), photoreceptor and visual-cycle genes (rpe65a, rdh5, rdh8a, stra6, rgrb, prom1b, and slc24a4a), and the pineal photoreceptor TF anchor otx5 supports annotation as pineal photoreceptors.  

**Distinguishing note:** 

This cluster is distinguished from retinal contamination by the absence of classic zebrafish retinal-lineage markers in your check and from non-photoreceptive pineal cell types by its combined photoreceptor, opsin, retinoid-handling, and melatonin-output signatures. One caution is that published zebrafish pineal literature usually treats aanat2 rather than aanat1 as the canonical pineal AANAT gene, so I would not let aanat1 carry the annotation by itself; the call is strongest because the rest of the cluster is overwhelmingly pineal-photoreceptor-like.  

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Pineal neuroendocrine / melatonin-output identity
    "asmt", "nfil3-6", "bhlhe40", "per2",
    "npas2", "tefa", "hlfa",

    # Direct pineal photosensitivity / opsin repertoire
    "opn4b", "opn4xa", "opn5",
    "opn7b", "opn8b", "opn9",

    # Photoreceptor structural and phototransduction machinery
    "prom1b", "rdh8a", "rpe65a",
    "rgrb", "rgra", "slc24a4a",
    "trpm1b", "myo7ab",

    # Retinoid-handling / visual-cycle-like program
    "rdh5", "stra6", "rbp5", "rbp4l",

    # Pineal transcription factor program
    "otx5", "lhx2b", "pax7a", "pax7b", "bsx"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
## Annotate peripheral clusters
### p1: Vascular endothelium

**Cluster 2: Vascular endothelium (arterial-leaning, non-lymphatic)**

One-line identity: Peripheral vascular endothelial cells defined by a strong pan-endothelial program with an arterial-leaning signature, lacking a dominant lymphatic/sinusoidal (LYVE1/MRC1/STAB) module (Bonkhofer et al., 2019; Hasan et al., 2017; Sacilotto et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2009).
 
**Key evidence**

• Core endothelial / vascular identity: ptprb, pecam1b, tie1, egfl7, rasip1
→ These genes establish the cluster as bona fide endothelium. Ptprb and pecam1b support endothelial identity, tie1 supports vascular endothelial specification, and egfl7 plus rasip1 are consistent with endothelial morphogenesis and vessel formation. 

• VEGF receptor endothelial backbone: kdr, kdrl, flt1
→ This receptor set reinforces that these are vascular endothelial cells responding to canonical endothelial growth-factor signaling. 

• Arterial-leaning endothelial specialization: dll4, erg, sox7, sox18, cxcr4a
→ dll4 is an arterial-leaning marker and erg supports a differentiated endothelial transcriptional program. 

• Endothelial junction / adhesion and vessel integrity: am2a, pcdh12
→ These genes support endothelial cell-cell adhesion and vessel organization. They help show this is a cohesive vascular endothelial population rather than hematopoietic carryover or stromal contamination.

• Additional vascular support / transport features: eng, slc2a1a, slc38a5b, nrp2a
→ These genes support a specialized vascular endothelial state. Eng fits best as vascular endothelium rather than junction-specific structure, while slc2a1a and slc38a5b suggest endothelial transport capacity, and nrp2a may indicate some non-arterial vascular heterogeneity layered onto the cluster.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a strong endothelial backbone (ptprb, pecam1b, tie1, egfl7, and rasip1) plus endothelial VEGF receptors (kdr, kdrl, and flt1) and a more limited but meaningful arterial-leaning module (dll4 and erg) supports annotation as vascular endothelium with arterial bias.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from lymphatic/scavenger endothelium by the absence of a dominant lyve1/mrc1/stab/flt4 DEG program, and from hemogenic endothelium by the lack of a coherent runx1/tal1/gata2/erythroid module in the DEG core. The dominant signal is vascular endothelium, with subtype information coming primarily from dll4 rather than from the generic endothelial markers themselves.

**Additional note:** 

Although non-BBB vascular endothelium is present in the brain, we have chosen to group this cell type as peripheral because there are no clear genetic markers to differentiate between brain vasculature and vasculature from other tissues that may have contaminated the dissection. This possibility makes any surface vs cave compositional analysis innacurate and so we have excluded this cluster from that calculation by classifying it as peripheral. 

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Core endothelial / vascular identity
    "ptprb", "pecam1b", "tie1", "egfl7", "rasip1",

    # VEGF receptor endothelial backbone
    "kdr", "kdrl", "flt1",

    # Arterial-leaning endothelial specialization
    "dll4", "erg", "sox7", "sox18", "cxcr4a",

    # Endothelial junction / adhesion and vessel integrity
    "jam2a", "pcdh12",

    # Additional vascular support / transport features
    "eng", "slc2a1a", "slc38a5b", "nrp2a"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### p2: Surface epithelium

**Cluster p2: Immune-responsive surface / mucosal epithelium**

One-line identity: Surface epithelial cells with a strong squamous–mucosal barrier program and a superimposed inflammatory / cytokine-responsive state, consistent with activated zebrafish surface ectoderm–derived epithelium rather than an immune-cell cluster (De La Garza et al., 2013; Jänicke et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2016; Mathiyalagan et al., 2025; Oehlers et al., 2010; Progatzky et al., 2016; Sarmah et al., 2022; Slanchev et al., 2009; Sommer et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021).  
 
**Key evidence**

•	Core epithelial / surface-barrier identity: krt5, krt99, ppl, evpla, evplb, scel, epcam, cldn7b, oclnb, grhl1, grhl3, elf3, tfap2c
→ The dominant signal is epithelial, not hematopoietic. In zebrafish, grhl1 marks periderm / epidermal epithelial populations, grhl3 is required for periderm differentiation downstream of irf6, epcam is required for epithelial morphogenesis and integrity during skin development, and elf3 is required for epidermal development.  

•	Junctional, polarity, and epithelial-sheet organization: cldn7b, oclnb, dsg2.1, epcam, mpp7a, pard3ba, rab25b, mal2, nectin4a, nectin4b
→ These genes fit a cohesive epithelial sheet with apical-basal polarity, junctional sealing, and membrane trafficking rather than a migratory immune population.  

•	Activated inflammatory / cytokine-responsive state layered on top of the epithelial identity: cxcl8a, il17rc, ifngr1, stat4, ripk2, traf2b, traf4a, ptgir, anxa1a, uba7
→ These are best interpreted as a response program, not a lineage program. In zebrafish, cxcl8 is induced by inflammatory stimulation and functions in inflammatory recruitment, and zebrafish mucosal epithelia such as the gill mount robust inflammatory responses at epithelial interfaces. So the immune-like genes here are most consistent with an activated epithelium sensing cytokines, damage, microbes, or environmental stress rather than true immune-cell identity. 

•	Surface squamous / mucosal specialization rather than neural, glial, or endothelial identity: upk3b, spint1a, spint1b, slc16a12b, aqp3a, slc17a9a, krt5, krt99, evplb, scel
→ The cluster lacks a coherent neuronal, glial, endothelial, or stromal backbone and instead shows the sort of structural and transport-associated profile expected of exposed barrier epithelia. 

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a strong epithelial structural and polarity program (krt5, krt99, ppl, evplb, scel, epcam, cldn7b, and oclnb), together with zebrafish-supported epithelial regulators (grhl1, grhl3, and elf3) and a secondary inflammatory-response module (cxcl8a, il17rc, ifngr1, stat4, andripk2) supports annotation as surface epithelial cells are not sitting in a quiet baseline state, but instead are responding to outside signals.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from true immune populations by the absence of a coherent leukocyte core and by the overwhelming dominance of epithelial barrier and differentiation genes. It is distinguished from generic quiescent surface epithelium by its added chemokine / cytokine-response signature. The dominant signal is therefore surface epithelial identity first, with immune-responsive activation state second.

```{r}

    "scel", "epcam", "cldn7b", "oclnb",
    "grhl1", "grhl3", "elf3", "tfap2c",

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```


### p3: Branchiomeric muscle

**Cluster 5: Branchiomeric skeletal muscle fibers**

One-line identity: Differentiated branchiomeric / head skeletal muscle fibers with a strong cardiopharyngeal lineage signal, defined by a complete sarcomeric contractile program, excitation–contraction coupling machinery, and neuromuscular-junction components, consistent with mature pharyngeal arch–derived striated muscle rather than cardiac, smooth, or progenitor muscle (Hinits et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2010; Olson et al., 2010; Ono et al., 2002; Paffett-Lugassy et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).  
 
**Key evidence**

• Fully differentiated striated muscle contractile apparatus: ttn.1, ttn.2, neb, myom1a, myom1b, myom2a, myom2b, myom3, obscna, obscnb, mybpc1, acta1b, actc1a, actc1b, myl1, myhb, myh7bb, tnnt1, tnnt3a, tnnt3b, actn3a, actn3b, ldb3a, ldb3b, nexn, dmd
→ This is an unequivocal skeletal myofiber program. The combination of titin, nebulin, myomesin, myosin, troponin, and actinin genes indicates mature contractile fibers, not a progenitor or stromal population.  

• Head / branchiomeric muscle lineage rather than generic trunk muscle: myf5, myod1, myog, mef2ca, mef2cb, nkx2.5
→ Zebrafish cranial muscle development uses myf5 and myod in a distinct way from trunk myogenesis. Branchiomeric muscles arise from cardiopharyngeal progenitors linked to nkx2.5-positive anterior lateral plate mesoderm. In zebrafish, pharyngeal arch 2 muscles specifically derive from nkx2.5+ progenitors, and mef2ca/mef2cb are required for skeletal muscle differentiation. 

• Excitation–contraction coupling machinery of mature skeletal fibers: ryr1a, ryr2b, ryr3, atp2a1, atp2a1l, cacna2d1a, jph1a, jph1b, jph2, trdn, atp1a2a, kcnj12b
→ These genes support functional calcium release, calcium reuptake, triad organization, and membrane excitability typical of differentiated muscle fibers. In zebrafish, ryr1a/ryr1b are required for skeletal muscle contraction and atp2a1 encodes SERCA1, which is essential for muscle relaxation. 

• Neuromuscular-junction specialization: colq, dok7b, rapsn, ache, jph1a, jph1b, jph2
→ This cluster also carries a neuromuscular-junction program. In zebrafish, rapsyn is essential for acetylcholine receptor clustering, and dok7 promotes neuromuscular-junction formation and muscle integrity, supporting annotation as innervated skeletal muscle fibers rather than immature myoblasts.  

• Metabolic and structural maturation consistent with terminally differentiated myofibers: ckma, ckmb, ak1, gyg1b, cpt1b, aldoab, eno3, ampd1, pfkfb3, coq10b
→ These genes support ATP buffering, glycogen handling, glycolysis, and oxidative metabolism typical of active mature muscle. The cluster is therefore best interpreted as differentiated muscle fibers, not a low-complexity or transitional state. 

**Decision rule:**

The combination of a complete skeletal sarcomere program (ttn, neb, myom, mybpc1, myosin, troponin, and actin genes), cardiopharyngeal / branchiomeric lineage markers (myf5, myod1, myog, mef2ca, mef2cb, and nkx2.5), mature calcium-handling machinery (ryr1a, atp2a1, and jph), and neuromuscular-junction components (dok7b, rapsn, colq, and ache) supports annotation as branchiomeric skeletal muscle fibers.  

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from cardiac muscle by its overwhelming skeletal sarcomeric and NMJ program, despite sharing some cardiopharyngeal-associated regulators such as nkx2.5 and mef2c paralogs. It is distinguished from smooth muscle / mural cells by the absence of a dominant acta2/myh11/tagln contractile signature and the presence instead of classic striated-muscle genes such as ttn, neb, mybpc1, ryr1a, and dok7b/rapsn. It is also distinguished from muscle progenitors by the heavy load of terminal structural and excitation–contraction genes, indicating a mature fiber state rather than a proliferative or early myogenic population.  

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Differentiated striated muscle contractile apparatus
    "ttn.1", "ttn.2", "neb",

    "obscna", "obscnb", "mybpc1",
```

### p4: Basal keratinocytes

**Cluster p4: Basal keratinocytes / epidermal basal cells**

One-line identity: Non-neural surface ectoderm–derived basal keratinocytes, defined by tp63/krt5 epithelial basal-cell identity together with hemidesmosome, laminin, collagen, integrin, and tight-junction genes that support attachment to the epidermal basement membrane (Esho et al., 2023; Fischer et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2014; Q. Li et al., 2011; Z. Liu et al., 2024; Molder et al., 2021; Phatak et al., 2021).
 
**Key evidence**

• Basal keratinocyte identity: krt5, krt8 (krt4), krt222, tp63, bnc1, fgfr2, itgb4
→ Integrin beta 4 (itgb4) is a basal-cell marker during growth, homeostasis, and injury response and tp63 is required for zebrafish epidermal appendage / keratinocyte renewal programs.  

• Basement membrane / hemidesmosome attachment program: col17a1a, col17a1b, col7a1, col7a1l, itgb4, itga6b, itga3b, lama5, lamb3, lamc2, lamb1a
→ These genes support a basal epithelial cell identity at the dermal–epidermal interface. In zebrafish, col17a1a is expressed in skin and type XVII collagen (col17a1a and col17a1b) is a hemidesmosome-associated basement membrane protein. Further, the α6β4 integrin–laminin system is a core hemidesmosome adhesion module linking basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane.  

• Epidermal barrier and junctional epithelial program: cldn1, cldni, epcam, jupa, ctnna1, ctnnd1, pard3aa, pard6gb, nectin1b, lsr
→ These genes support epithelial polarity, adhesion, and barrier organization rather than neural, endothelial, or mesenchymal identity. Zebrafish skin has a defined epidermis separated from the dermis by a basement membrane zone that fits the epithelial-barrier context of these markers.  

• Epidermal transcriptional regulation: grhl2b, irf6, tp63, tfap2c, dlx3b, dlx4a
→ The grainyhead-like (grhl2b) program is strongly associated with zebrafish epidermal development and barrier maintenance. Grhl3 promotes epidermal cell retention and architecture, and irf6–grhl3 work supports a conserved keratinocyte/periderm differentiation program.  

• Dermal–epidermal junction / anchoring complex: fras1, frem2a, frem2b, col7a1, col7a1l
→ The fras1/frem2 module supports a skin basement membrane / dermal–epidermal junction context. Fraser-complex proteins are associated with anchoring structures at the dermal–epidermal junction, which fits the basal keratinocyte interpretation.  

**Decision rule:**

The combination of tp63/krt5 basal epithelial identity, itgb4/itga6b/laminin/col17a1/col7a1 basement membrane attachment machinery, epithelial junction genes, and Fraser-complex dermal–epidermal junction genes supports annotation as basal keratinocytes / epidermal basal cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from superficial/mucosal epithelium by its stronger basal attachment program: col17a1a/b, col7a1/col7a1l, itgb4, itga6b, lama5, lamb3, lamc2. It is distinguished from fibroblasts by epithelial keratin and junction genes, and from neural/glial/endothelial populations by the absence of a coherent neuronal, glial, or vascular marker program.

```{r}
    # Basal keratinocyte identity
    "krt5", "krt8", "krt222",
    "tp63", "bnc1", "fgfr2", "itgb4",

    # Basement membrane / hemidesmosome attachment
    "col17a1a", "col17a1b", "col7a1", "col7a1l",
    "itga6b", "itga3b",
    "lama5", "lamb3", "lamc2", "lamb1a",

    # Epidermal barrier / junctional program
    "cldn1", "cldni", "epcam", "jupa",
    "ctnna1", "ctnnd1", "pard3aa",
    "pard6gb", "nectin1b", "lsr",

    "grhl2b", "irf6", "tfap2c", "dlx3b", "dlx4a",

    "fras1", "frem2a", "frem2b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
