### p5: Erythrocytes

**Cluster p5: Erythrocytes / red blood cells**

One-line identity: Mature erythrocytes, defined by a coherent erythroid transcriptional program, heme/iron-handling machinery, hemoglobin-associated oxygen transport genes, and red-cell membrane/cytoskeletal components (Chen et al., 2020; Gore et al., 2018; K. Kim et al., 2025; Suzuki et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021).
 
**Key evidence**

• Erythroid lineage and maturation program: gata1a, klf1, cbfa2t3, jak2a, rpl18
→ These genes support erythroid identity rather than generic blood contamination. Zebrafish erythropoiesis depends on erythroid transcriptional regulators, like gata1a, while klf1/klf17 are involved in erythroid maturation.  

• Heme synthesis, iron handling, and hemoglobin-associated function: alas2, slc25a37, slc25a39, fech, tfr1a, ncoa4, fth1a, hbbe1.1
→ These genes indicate hemoglobin-producing erythroid cells:  alas2 is an erythroid heme-synthesis enzyme, mitoferrin (slc25a37) supports mitochondrial iron import for heme production, and hbbe1.1 is an embryonic β-globin gene used as a zebrafish erythroid marker. 

• Red blood cell membrane and cytoskeletal scaffold: slc4a1a, ank1a, sptb, add2, rhag
→ slc4a1a encodes the Band 3/anion-exchanger erythrocyte membrane protein, ank1a, sptb, and add2 support the specialized erythrocyte membrane skeleton.  

• Oxidative-stress buffering and red-cell metabolism: prdx2, gpx1a, gpx4b, aldoa/aldob-associated glycolytic program, cahz
→ Hemoglobin-rich erythrocytes require strong antioxidant and metabolic buffering. This function is mediated through expression of genes such as prdx2 and gpx1a/gpx4b that support ROS handling. In addition, cahz and slc4a1a support CO₂/bicarbonate transport and erythrocyte gas-exchange physiology.

• Ion and volume regulation: kcnn4, slc4a1a, wnk2, wnk4b, slc9a1b
→ These genes support mature red-cell membrane physiology. For example, kcnn4 is likely involved in erythrocyte ion/volume regulation.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of erythroid regulators (gata1a and klf1), heme/iron genes (alas2, slc25a37, fech, and tfr1a), globin-associated identity (hbbe1.1), and RBC membrane scaffold genes (slc4a1a, ank1a, sptb, and add2) supports annotation as erythrocytes / red blood cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from endothelial or vascular-associated cells by its dominant erythroid membrane and heme-production program, and from hematopoietic progenitors by the strong mature RBC scaffold and oxygen-transport machinery. The dominant signal is mature circulating erythrocytes, not a mixed blood progenitor population.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Erythroid lineage and maturation program
    "gata1a", "klf1", "cbfa2t3", "jak2a", "rpl18",

    # Heme synthesis, iron handling, and hemoglobin-associated function
    "alas2", "slc25a37", "slc25a39",
    "fech", "tfr1a", "ncoa4", "fth1a", "hbbe1.1",

    # Red blood cell membrane and cytoskeletal scaffold
    "slc4a1a", "ank1a", "sptb", "add2", "rhag",

    # Oxidative-stress buffering and red-cell metabolism
    "prdx2", "gpx1a", "gpx4b",
    "aldoa", "aldob", "cahz",

    # Ion and volume regulation
    "kcnn4", "wnk2", "wnk4b", "slc9a1b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### p6: Chondrocytes

**Cluster p6: Chondrocytes**

One-line identity: Matrix-producing chondrocytes, defined by sox9a/sox5/sox6 cartilage regulatory genes together with strong cartilage ECM, proteoglycan, collagen-processing, and chondrocyte signaling programs (Baas et al., 2009; Giovannone et al., 2019; He et al., 2016; Lawrence et al., 2018; Smeeton et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2002; Yokoi et al., 2009).
 
**Key evidence**

• Core cartilage matrix identity: col2a1a, col9a1a, col9a2, col9a3, col11a1a, col11a2, col27a1a, col27a1b, acana, acanb, matn1, matn4, epyc, snorc, hapln1b
→ Zebrafish chondrocyte populations are defined by cartilage matrix genes such as col2a1a, acana/acanb and collagen II/XI/IX-family genes.  

• Chondrocyte regulatory transcription factors: sox9a, sox5, sox6, mef2ab
→ These genes differentiate this cartilage cluster from a generic ECM-producing mesenchymal population. Sox9a is required for zebrafish cartilage morphogenesis and overt cartilage differentiation, while sox5/sox6 support the chondrogenic program with Sox9-family activity. 

• Proteoglycan and glycosaminoglycan synthesis / matrix assembly: xylt1, chsy1, chsy3, chst3b, chst7, csgalnact1a, papss2b, ugdh, slc35d1a
→ These genes support cartilage proteoglycan and chondroitin sulfate matrix production. This is important because the cluster is not just collagen-rich; it has the glycosaminoglycan biosynthetic machinery expected for cartilage ECM.

• Collagen processing and matrix maturation: adamts3, p4ha2, p4ha1a, p3h2, lo xl3b, lo xl2a, serpinh1b, fkbp10b, colgalt1b, colgalt2b
→ These genes support active collagen modification, folding, and matrix remodeling. Together with the collagen/proteoglycan core, this indicates actively matrix-producing chondrocytes rather than contaminating connective tissue.

• Cartilage growth / maturation signaling: fgfr3, fgfrl1b, bmpr1bb, pth1r, npr2, ccn2a, ccn6, thbs1b, trpv4
→ These genes are consistent with chondrocyte maturation, cartilage growth control, and matrix homeostasis. Zebrafish jaw cartilage regeneration studies identify chondrocyte clusters with mature and immature cartilage programs, supporting this type of transcriptional subdivision within cartilage.  

**Decision rule:**

The combination of sox9a, sox5, and sox6 cartilage regulatory genes, strong cartilage collagens (col2a1a, col9a1a/2/3, and col11a1a/2), proteoglycan matrix genes (acana, acanb, hapln1b, epyc, and snorc), and cartilage matrix-processing machinery supports annotation as chondrocytes.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from fibroblasts by its cartilage-specific matrix program, especially col2a1a, col9a genes, col11a genes, acana/acanb, matn1, and sox9a. It is distinguished from osteoblast-like cells by the absence of a dominant mineralizing bone program and by the strong chondrogenic Sox9/collagen II/aggrecan signature. The dominant signal is matrix-producing cartilage, not generic mesenchyme.

### p7: OSNs

**Cluster p7: Olfactory sensory neurons**

One-line identity: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), most consistent with mature ciliated/odorant-transduction OSNs, defined by olfactory G-protein signaling genes, sensory transduction machinery, ciliary/axon-associated genes, and neuronal synaptic/axon guidance features (Bergboer et al., 2018; Calvo-Ochoa et al., 2021; W. Chen et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2005; Shao et al., 2017).
 
**Key evidence**

• Mature ciliated olfactory sensory neuron identity: ompa, gnal, gng13b, gnao1b, rgs11, adcy8, ano2b, pde1ca, pde1cb, pde4ba
→ These genes support mature ciliated OSN identity. Ompa supports mature OSNs, while gnal/gng13b/gnao1b, adcy8, ano2b, PDE genes, and rgs11 support olfactory signal transduction downstream of odorant receptor activation.


• Sensory cilium structure / intraflagellar transport: ift122, ift172, ift80, ift81, ift88, ift140, ift27, tulp3, rfx3, rpgrip1l, tmem67, bbs7
→ These genes support the ciliated sensory apparatus required for olfactory detection. 

• Chemosensory / GPCR-associated signaling: gpr158a, gpr137bb, rxfp2a, drd2a, drd2b, adcyap1b, gabbr1a
→ These genes support a receptor-rich sensory-neuron identity. In zebrafish olfactory epithelium, OSN subtypes are organized around distinct receptor and GPCR-linked transduction programs, including OR/TAAR-associated ciliated OSNs and other chemosensory OSN classes.  

• Axon guidance / olfactory projection features: cntn4, cntnap5a, dcc, unc5a, unc5b, epha6, efna2a, flrt1a, flrt1b, l1cama, l1camb, ncam1b, robo2
→ These genes support sensory neurons that project axons to olfactory bulb targets. Zebrafish OSNs project from the olfactory epithelium to defined olfactory bulb glomeruli/protoglomeruli. 

• Neuronal differentiation / synaptic machinery: syt1a, syt7a, syt17, snap25b, cadpsa, cadpsb, rims1b, rims3, unc13a, pp fia2, cacna1ba, cacna1db, scn1lab, scn5lab, kcna3a, kcna4, gng8, 
→ These genes confirm that the cluster is neuronal and synaptically competent, not a supporting epithelial, mesenchymal, immune, or glial population.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of olfactory transduction genes, especially gnal, gng13b, gnao1b, rgs11, ano2b, adcy8, and PDE genes, together with ompa and many ciliary/IFT genes, supports annotation as olfactory sensory neurons.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from inner-ear/otic sensory cells by the dominant olfactory G-protein/transduction signature, especially gnal and gng13b, and also by OSN-associated ciliary and axon-guidance programs.

### p8: Skeletal muscle

**Cluster p8: Myocytes**

One-line identity: Mature skeletal muscle / myofiber cluster, defined by a strong sarcomere-contractile program, excitation–contraction coupling machinery, muscle membrane/costamere components, and myogenic structural assembly factors (Chong et al., 2020; Ferrante et al., 2011; Ha et al., 2013; Horstick et al., 2013; Sztal et al., 2015).
 
**Key evidence**

• Sarcomere / contractile myofiber core: mylpfb, mylpfa, myl1, ttn.1, ttn.2, neb, tnnt3a, tnnt3b, acta1b, actc1a, actc1b, mybpc1, myom1a, myom1b, myom2a, myom2b, myoz1b, myot, obscnb, xirp2a, xirp2b
→ This cluster is dominated by myofibrillar and sarcomere genes, including titin, nebulin, actin, troponin, myosin light chain, myosin-binding, myomesin, and Z-disc/costamere-associated genes.

• Excitation–contraction coupling / calcium handling: atp2a1l, stac3, ryr3, jph1a, jph1b, calm1b, calm2a, calm3a, calm3b, slc25a4, slc25a5
→ These genes support functional contractile myofibers with calcium cycling and excitation–contraction machinery. Atp2a1l/SERCA-like calcium handling, ryanodine receptor expression, and junctophilin genes are consistent with mature muscle calcium-release and sarcoplasmic-reticulum organization. 

• Muscle membrane / structural anchoring program: xirp2a, xirp2b, myot, prx, rtn4b, rtn2a, tmod4, capza1b, flot1b
→ These support structural stabilization of the contractile apparatus and muscle membrane-associated architecture. This is consistent with differentiated myofibers rather than generic mesenchymal or epithelial cells.

• Myofiber assembly and remodeling factors: hacd1, trim63a, mylk3, ckma, ckmb, ckmt1, ckmt2b, pygmb
→ These genes support mature muscle assembly, contractile maintenance, and muscle energy buffering. Creatine kinase genes and glycogen/metabolic genes fit an energetically active contractile cell type.

• Metabolic support for contractile muscle: aco2, idh2, cs, dlst, dldh, pdha1a, pdhb, mdh2, got2a, ndufa genes, ndufb genes, ndufs genes, atp5 genes, vdac2, vdac3
→ This broad mitochondrial/TCA/oxidative phosphorylation signature is consistent with the high energetic demand of differentiated myofibers.

• Fiber-type: mylpfb, mylpfa, tnnt3a, tnnt3b, actn3a, actn3b, pvalb6, ckmb, myh7bb 
→ The DEG list is strongly compatible with skeletal myofibers, with fast-fiber-associated markers such as mylpf/tnnt3/actn3/pvalb6. 

**Decision rule:**

The combination of sarcomere genes, especially mylpfb, ttn.1, ttn.2, tnnt3a, neb, acta1b, actc1a/b, mybpc1, myom genes, myoz1b, myot, and xirp2a/b, together with calcium-handling and muscle metabolic genes, supports annotation as mature skeletal muscle / myofibers.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from muscle progenitors by the dominance of differentiated contractile genes rather than primarily myod1/myf5/myog-like regulatory genes. It is distinguished from fibroblasts or tendon/connective tissue by the overwhelming sarcomere program. It is also not cardiac muscle despite actc1a/b and tnnt-like genes, because the broader signature includes skeletal muscle-associated mylpf, tnnt3, acta1b, actn3, neb, ttn, and fast-fiber/metabolic markers.

### p9: LL support cells

**Cluster p9: Lateral-line supporting cells**

One-line identity: Lateral-line neuromast supporting/progenitor epithelial cells, defined by lateral-line signaling and patterning genes together with epithelial junction/adhesion genes, partial hair-cell–associated sensory-organ markers, and absence of a strong otic matrix or mature mechanosensory hair-cell program (Han et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2023).
 
**Key evidence**

• Lateral-line support cell program: tfap2a, fgfr1a, cxcr4b, fat1b, tnfsf10l3,
→ These genes support lateral-line neuromast identity rather than generic epithelium: cxcr4b is strongly associated with lateral-line primordium migration, fgfr1a fits signaling-active neuromast progenitor/supporting-cell states, and tfap2a supports cranial placodal/lateral-line sensory epithelial identity.

• Supporting-cell / epithelial identity: krt18b, krt1-c5, grhl2a, grhl2b, cdh2, gjc4b, itgb5, col7a1, kirrel3l, ctnna1
→ These genes support a polarized epithelial/supporting-cell population rather than neurons or mature hair cells. The keratin, Grainyhead-like, cadherin/catenin, connexin, integrin, and basement-membrane-associated genes indicate epithelial organization and adhesion.

• Hair-cell-associated sensory-organ context: ush1c, cadm4, prom1a, syt14a, cbln18, cbln20
→ These genes place the cluster within a hair-cell-containing sensory organ environment. However, the DEG list is not dominated by mature mechanotransduction/hair-bundle genes, so these are best interpreted as sensory-organ association rather than mature hair-cell identity.

• Against otic matrix / inner-ear epithelial identity: absence of sox10, stm, otog, otogl, otomp, tecta
→ The lack of strong otic matrix and otic epithelial genes weakens an inner-ear sensory epithelium annotation and supports a lateral-line neuromast supporting-cell identity instead.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of lateral-line-associated signaling genes, especially tfap2a, cxcr4b, fgfr1a, and fat1b, with epithelial junction/adhesion genes and only partial hair-cell-associated signal supports annotation as lateral-line supporting cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from mature hair cells by the absence of a dominant mechanotransduction and stereocilia program. It is distinguished from otic sensory epithelium by the lack of strong otic matrix genes such as otog, otogl, otomp, and tecta. The dominant signal is lateral-line sensory epithelial support/progenitor identity, not mature hair-cell identity.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Lateral-line support cell program
    "tfap2a", "fgfr1a", "cxcr4b",
    "fat1b", "tnfsf10l3",

    # Supporting-cell / epithelial identity
    "krt18b", "krt1-c5",
    "grhl2a", "grhl2b",
    "cdh2", "gjc4b", "itgb5",
    "col7a1", "kirrel3l", "ctnna1",

    # Hair-cell-associated sensory-organ context
    "ush1c", "cadm4", "prom1a",
    "syt14a", "cbln18", "cbln20"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### p10: Otic support cells

**Cluster p10: Otic sensory epithelium / otolith-matrix supporting cells**

One-line identity: Inner-ear otic sensory epithelium / otolith-associated supporting cells, defined by strong otolith/tectorial-matrix genes, otic epithelial structural genes, and inner-ear patterning factors, with limited mature hair-cell mechanotransduction signal (Murayama et al., 2005; Shi et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2023; Söllner et al., 2003, 2004; Stooke-Vaughan et al., 2015).
 
**Key evidence**

• Otolith / tectorial-matrix identity: stm, otomp, otog, tectb, zpld1a, col9a1a, col9a1b, col9a2, col9a3, col11a2, col2a1a
→ These genes support an inner-ear otic epithelial identity: stm is a zebrafish otolith biomineralization gene; otog and α-tectorin/tecta are required for otolith tethering to the sensory macula, and otomp/OMP-1 and otolin genes are required for normal otolith growth and anchoring onto sensory maculae.

• Otic epithelial structure / supporting-cell features: magi2a, itga6a, pard6b, cdh7a, kirrel1b, nphs1
→ These genes support epithelial polarity, adhesion, and junctional organization typical of sensory epithelia rather than neurons.

• Otic patterning / epithelial morphogenesis: lmx1ba, lmx1bb, wnt3, sfrp1a, ryk, ptk7a, dacha, epha4a, epha4l
→ These genes support otic vesicle patterning and spatial organization of sensory vs non-sensory domains. lmx1ba/lmx1bb in particular indicate inner-ear epithelial patterning, reinforcing that this is a structured otic tissue rather than generic epithelium.

• Sensory-organ (hearing/vestibular) context without mature hair-cell identity: ush2a
→ ush2a links the cluster to a hearing-related sensory system, but the DEG list lacks dominant mechanotransduction and stereocilia genes (e.g., tmc, myo7aa, cdh23, pcdh15a, espn, slc17a8). This indicates association with the sensory organ without being the mature mechanosensory hair cells themselves.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of stm, otomp, otog, tectb, otic matrix collagens, and lmx1ba/lmx1bb supports annotation as inner-ear otic sensory epithelium / otolith-matrix supporting cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from lateral-line supporting cells by the strong otolith/otic-matrix program, especially stm, otog, otomp, and tectb. It is distinguished from mature hair cells by the lack of a dominant mechanotransduction and stereocilia program. The dominant signal is inner-ear otolith-associated sensory epithelium/supporting cells, not lateral line and not mature hair cells.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Otolith / tectorial-matrix identity
    "stm", "otomp", "otog", "tectb",
    "zpld1a",
    "col9a1a", "col9a1b", "col9a2", "col9a3",
    "col11a2", "col2a1a",

    # Otic epithelial structure / supporting-cell features
    "magi2a", "itga6a", "pard6b",
    "cdh7a", "kirrel1b", "nphs1",

    "dacha",

    # Sensory-organ context
    "ush2a"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### p11: Schwann cells

**Cluster p11: Schwann cells**

One-line identity: Myelinating peripheral Schwann cells, defined by a strong PNS glial/myelin program, Schwann-associated adhesion genes, ErbB signaling, and nodal/axo-glial organization genes (Eshed et al., 2005; Heermann et al., 2011; Konrad et al., 2006; Lyons et al., 2005; Raphael et al., 2010; Raphael & Talbot, 2011).
 
**Key evidence**

• Core Schwann / peripheral glial identity: cdh19, cldn19, erbb2, erbb3a, erbb3b, pou3f1, sox2, sox10
→ These genes support Schwann-cell identity rather than CNS oligodendrocytes. erbb2/erbb3 signaling is required for Schwann cell migration and myelination in zebrafish, while cdh19, cldn19, and pou3f1 fit peripheral glial/Schwann differentiation and myelinating Schwann-cell maturation. 

• Myelin sheath program: mbpa, mbpb, mag, bcas1, qki2, gal3st1a, abca2
→ These genes support a myelinating glial state: mbp expression marks myelinating glia in zebrafish, including Schwann cells along peripheral nerves, while mag, qki, gal3st1, and abca2 support myelin membrane organization and lipid-rich sheath production. 

• Axo-glial junction / nodal organization: gldn, nfascb, cntn1a, cntn2, drp2, ank2b, cdh6
→ These genes support peripheral axon–glia organization: gldn/gliomedin and neurofascin/contactin-family adhesion molecules are central to nodal and paranodal architecture at myelinated axons, while drp2 is consistent with Schwann-cell myelin-associated dystroglycan/periaxin-type organization. 

• ErbB / axon-dependent Schwann signaling: erbb2, erbb3a, erbb3b, tgfbr2b, gfra4b, prkg2, paqr6
→ This signaling profile fits Schwann cells interacting with peripheral axons. In zebrafish, erbb2 and erbb3 are required for Schwann cell development, migration.

• Schwann-cell adhesion / basal-lamina-associated support: itgb1a, itgb6, tln2b, chst7, smoc2, olfml2a, gpc5c, jupb, plekha7a, plekha7b, rac1b
→ These genes support the adhesive and extracellular-supportive character of Schwann cells. Schwann cells form peripheral nerve-associated glial sheaths and interact closely with axons and surrounding matrix, so this adhesion/ECM program fits myelinating PNS glia rather than CNS oligodendrocytes.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of cdh19, cldn19, and erbb2/erbb3a/erbb3b, strong myelin genes (mbpa, mbpb, mag, bcas1, qki2, and gal3st1a), and nodal/axo-glial genes (gldn, nfascb, cntn1a, cntn2, and drp2) supports annotation as myelinating Schwann cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from CNS oligodendrocytes by the Schwann/PNS-associated genes cdh19, cldn19, erbb2/erbb3, drp2, and gldn, together with the peripheral axo-glial/nodal program. Although several myelin genes are shared with oligodendrocytes, the dominant signal is peripheral Schwann-cell myelination rather than CNS oligodendrocyte identity.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Core Schwann / peripheral glial identity
    "cdh19", "cldn19",
    "erbb2", "erbb3a", "erbb3b",
    "pou3f1", "sox2", "sox10",

    # Myelin sheath program
    "mbpa", "mbpb", "mag", "bcas1",
    "qki2", "gal3st1a", "abca2",

    # Axo-glial junction / nodal organization
    "gldn", "nfascb", "cntn1a", "cntn2",
    "drp2", "ank2b", "cdh6",

    # ErbB / axon-dependent Schwann signaling
    "tgfbr2b", "gfra4b", "prkg2", "paqr6",

    # Schwann-cell adhesion / basal-lamina support
    "itgb1a", "itgb6", "tln2b",
    "chst7", "smoc2", "olfml2a", "gpc5c",
    "jupb", "plekha7a", "plekha7b", "rac1b"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```

### p12: Pituitary endocrine

**Cluster 17: Pituitary endocrine cells**

One-line identity: Mixed adenohypophyseal endocrine cells, defined by pituitary developmental transcription factors, multiple hormone lineages, and neuroendocrine secretory-processing machinery (Herzog et al., 2003; N. A. Liu et al., 2003; Nica et al., 2004; D. Wang et al., 2017; C. Y. Yan et al., 2023).
 
**Key evidence**

• Pituitary developmental / adenohypophyseal identity: pou1f1, lhx3, pitx3, six3a, insm1a, neurod1
→ These genes support adenohypophyseal endocrine identity: pou1f1/pit1, lhx3, and pitx3 are central pituitary developmental markers in zebrafish. Pou1f1, specifically, is required for somatotroph, lactotroph, and thyrotroph lineages. 

• Mixed pituitary hormone lineages: gh1, prl, pomca
→ These genes identify multiple endocrine lineages within the adenohypophysis: gh1 marks somatotrophs, prl marks lactotrophs, and pomca marks corticotroph/melanotroph-lineage cells. The co-enrichment of multiple hormone genes supports a mixed pituitary endocrine cluster rather than a single pure hormone subtype.

• Neuroendocrine secretory / hormone-processing machinery: scg3, pcsk2, cpe, ptprn2, baiap3, rab3da, rab3db, snap25b, stx1a, cplx2, doc2b
→ These genes support a secretory endocrine/neuroendocrine state: pcsk2 and cpe are consistent with peptide hormone processing, while scg3, rab3, snap25b, stx1a, and cplx2 support regulated dense-core vesicle secretion. 

• Pituitary responsiveness / GPCR and calcium signaling: vipr2, sstr3, adcyap1r1b, avpr2ab, htr7c, oprd1a, ntsr1, pth2ra, trpc4a, cacna1db, cacna1bb, cacna2d1a
→ These genes fit hormone-responsive endocrine cells with receptor-linked calcium/cAMP signaling. This supports an active pituitary endocrine population rather than structural epithelium or neuronal contamination.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of pituitary developmental transcription factors (pou1f1, lhx3, and pitx3), multiple hormone genes (gh1, prl, and pomca), and neuroendocrine secretory-processing genes (scg3, pcsk2, cpe, ptprn2, snap25b, and stx1a) supports annotation as mixed adenohypophyseal pituitary endocrine cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from hypothalamic neurons by the pituitary hormone genes gh1, prl, and pomca together with pou1f1,lhx3, and pitx3. It is distinguished from generic neuroendocrine cells by the adenohypophyseal hormone-lineage program. The dominant signal is mixed pituitary endocrine identity.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Pituitary developmental / adenohypophyseal identity
    "pou1f1", "lhx3", "pitx3",
    "six3a", "insm1a", "neurod1",

    # Mixed pituitary hormone lineages
    "gh1", "prl", "pomca",

    # Neuroendocrine secretory / hormone-processing machinery
    "scg3", "pcsk2", "cpe", "ptprn2",
    "baiap3", "rab3da", "rab3db",
    "snap25b", "stx1a", "cplx2", "doc2b",

    # Pituitary responsiveness / GPCR and calcium signaling
    "vipr2", "sstr3", "adcyap1r1b", "avpr2ab",
    "htr7c", "oprd1a", "ntsr1", "pth2ra",
    "trpc4a", "cacna1db", "cacna1bb", "cacna2d1a"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```
### p13: Cranial sensory neurons

**Cluster 20: Pitx2⁺ / Lhx9⁺ cranial sensory neurons**

One-line identity: Cranial sensory ganglion-like neurons, most consistent with epibranchial/visceral sensory neurons, defined by cranial sensory neuronal transcription factors, glutamatergic identity, strong axon-guidance/adhesion genes, and mature synaptic machinery (Andermann et al., 2002; Dam et al., 2011; Y. Liu & Semina, 2012; McGraw et al., 2012; Nechiporuk et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2012).
 
**Key evidence**

• Cranial sensory / epibranchial ganglion context: pitx2, lhx9, lhx1a, scrt2, pou2f2a, fgf8a
→  This gene combination supports cranial sensory ganglion identity rather than CNS neurons. Cranial sensory neurons in zebrafish arise from cranial placodes (epibranchial/trigeminal), not the neural tube, and are defined by distinct TF programs from CNS neurons. 

• Glutamatergic sensory neuron identity: slc17a6a, grin3ba, gria1a, gria2b, gria3b, gria4b, grin1b, grin2aa, grin2ab, grin2da, grm8a, grm8b
→ These genes support an excitatory glutamatergic neuronal identity: slc17a6a encodes a vesicular glutamate transporter used to identify glutamatergic neurons in zebrafish, while the AMPA/NMDA/metabotropic glutamate receptor genes support glutamate-responsive sensory neurons. 

• Cranial sensory axon guidance / adhesion program: robo2, unc5da, celsr3, sema4e, cntnap5l, lrrc24, tenm2b, clstn2b, fstl4
→ These genes support a projection-neuron identity with active axon guidance and sensory-ganglion wiring features: robo2 is expressed in zebrafish trigeminal ganglion sensory neurons and controls subtype-specific axonal projections, while unc5-family genes and semaphorin/cadherin/adhesion genes fit axon pathfinding and target selection.

• Synaptic and mature neuronal machinery: sypa, sypb, vamp2, snap91a, rph3ab, stxbp5a, gap43, dpysl2a, dpysl2b, caskin2
→ These genes support mature neuronal synaptic/axon-growth identity: gap43 and synaptic vesicle genes are consistent with differentiated sensory neurons rather than placodal epithelium or glia.

• Sensory-modulatory receptor profile: oprl1, npffr2a, qrfprb, adcyap1r1b, gabrg2, gpr183b
→ These genes support a neuromodulatory sensory-neuron state. They are best treated as supporting evidence for sensory responsiveness and interoceptive/visceral-like modulation, not as primary lineage markers.

**Decision rule:**

The combination of cranial sensory neuronal markers (pitx2, lhx9, lhx1a, scrt2, pou2f2a), glutamatergic identity (slc17a6a and glutamate receptor genes), and a strong axon-guidance/adhesion program (robo2, unc5da, celsr3, sema4e, cntnap5l) supports annotation as Pitx2⁺ / Lhx9⁺ cranial sensory neurons, most consistent with epibranchial/visceral sensory neurons.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is excluded from CNS neuron groups because it lacks any defining CNS regional transcriptional identity and instead expresses a cranial placode–derived sensory neuron program. The dominant signal is peripheral cranial sensory ganglion identity, not central nervous system neuron identity.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    "pitx2", "lhx9", "lhx1a",
    "scrt2", "pou2f2a", "fgf8a", 

    # Glutamatergic sensory neuron identity
    "slc17a6a",
    "grin3ba",
    "gria1a", "gria2b", "gria3b", "gria4b",
    "grin1b", "grin2aa", "grin2ab", "grin2da",
    "grm8a", "grm8b",

    "cntnap5l", "lrrc24", "tenm2b", "clstn2b", "fstl4",
```

### p14: Hepatocytes

**Cluster p14: Hepatocytes**

One-line identity: Hepatocyte-like / liver-derived population, defined by liver-enriched metabolic transcriptional programs, apolipoprotein/lipid transport genes, plasma/coagulation/complement genes, gluconeogenic and amino-acid metabolism enzymes, and bile/organic-anion transporters (Anderson et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2022; Mo et al., 2024; Moll & Farber, 2024).
 
**Key evidence**

• Liver / hepatocyte-enriched metabolic identity: hnf4b, nr5a2, nr1h5, prox1a, onecut2, klf15, foxo1a, pparab
→ These transcription factors and nuclear receptors support a hepatocyte-like metabolic identity rather than a brain-resident cell type. 

• Hepatocyte lipid transport / liver-enriched markers: fabp10a, gc, bhmt, tfa, foxa3, apoa1b, apoba, apoa2, apoc1, apom, ldlra, slc27a1a, slc27a2a, slc27a6, scp2a, soat2
→ These genes strongly support liver/hepatocyte identity. Apolipoprotein and fatty-acid transport genes are core zebrafish liver/hepatocyte features and zebrafish liver studies use hepatocyte lipid-transport programs, including apolipoproteins and fatty-acid binding/transport genes, to identify liver-derived cells.

• Plasma proteins, coagulation, and complement: c3b.1, c4b, c5, cfi, f5, f10, fgb, fgg, plg, fetub, ahsg2, itih2
→ This secreted plasma-protein signature is highly consistent with hepatocytes. The liver is the major source of many coagulation, complement, and circulating plasma proteins. 

• Gluconeogenesis / carbohydrate and amino-acid metabolism: g6pc1a.2, pck1, pck2, gys2, aldob, gnmt, bhmt, mat1a, tat, pah, agxtb, hal, fah, tdo2b
→ These genes support hepatocyte metabolic function and code for enzymes involved in glucose production, glycogen metabolism, one-carbon/amino-acid metabolism, tyrosine/phenylalanine metabolism, and nitrogen handling.

• Bile acid / organic anion and hepatocyte transporter program: abcb11b, abcc12, slco1d1, slco2a1, slc2a2, slc13a5a, aqp9b, atp7b
→ These genes support liver transport and hepatocyte-like physiology: abcb11 is a bile salt export transporter, slco genes support organic-anion transport, and slc2a2/aqp9b fit hepatocyte nutrient and small-solute transport. 

**Decision rule:**

The combination of liver metabolic regulators, apolipoprotein/lipid transport genes, plasma/coagulation/complement genes, gluconeogenic and amino-acid metabolism enzymes, and bile/organic-anion transporters supports annotation as hepatocytes / liver-derived cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from brain-resident cell types by the absence of neuronal, glial, epithelial sensory, immune, or vascular marker programs and by the dominance of hepatocyte functions, such as lipid transport, plasma protein secretion, complement/coagulation production, gluconeogenesis, amino-acid metabolism, and bile/organic-anion transport. The dominant signal is liver-derived hepatocyte contamination, not a larval brain cell type.

```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Liver / hepatocyte-enriched metabolic identity
    "hnf4b", "nr5a2", "nr1h5", "prox1a",
    "onecut2", "klf15", "foxo1a", "pparab",

    # Hepatocyte lipid transport / liver-enriched markers

    "f5", "f10", "fgb", "fgg",
    "plg", "fetub", "ahsg2", "itih2",
```

### p15: Mechanosensory hair cells

**Cluster 23: Mechanosensory hair cells**

One-line identity: Mature mechanosensory hair cells from inner ear and/or lateral line, defined by canonical mechanotransduction/tip-link genes, stereocilia myosin and actin-bundle genes, ciliary/kinociliary machinery, and ribbon-synapse neurotransmission genes (Chatterjee et al., 2015; Ebrahim et al., 2016; Fang et al., 2015; Manchanda et al., 2019; Nicolson, 2015; Qian et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2020, 2023).
 
**Key evidence**

• Mechanotransduction / tip-link machinery: tmc1, tmc2a, tmc2b, cdh23, pcdh15a, pcdh15b, cabp2b, ptprq
→ These genes support mature hair-cell identity: tmc2a/tmc2b are required for hair-cell mechanotransduction, cdh23 and pcdh15 are tip-link-associated genes, and cabp2b is also expressed in hair cells.

• Stereocilia / hair-bundle structure: myo6b, myo7aa, myo15aa, myo15ab, myo15b, myo3b, espn, whrna, ripor2, ush1c
→ These genes support the specialized actin-rich hair bundle: myo7aa, myo15, and related stereocilia genes are core hair-cell structural genes and myosin/espin-associated machinery is directly linked to stereocilia organization.  

• Hair-cell ribbon synapse / neurotransmission: otofa, slc17a8, cacna1da, cacna1db, rims2a, rims2b, pcloa, pclob, rab3ab, syt14a
→ These genes support mature synaptic hair-cell function: otofa is required for hair-cell synaptic function, cacna1da/Cav1.3a is a classic zebrafish hair-cell ribbon-synapse calcium channel, and slc17a8 is part of the zebrafish hair-cell neurotransmission program.  

• Ciliary / kinocilium and axonemal program: dnah5, dnah7, dnah9, dnah9l, dnah2, cfap58, ift172, ift80, ift122, ift140, dync2i1, bbs9, rfx2, pacrg, hydin
→ These genes support the ciliary/axonemal component of hair-cell sensory architecture, including kinocilium-associated and intraflagellar transport machinery. Zebrafish hair-cell single-cell data identify ciliary and hair-cell structural programs across inner-ear hair-cell subtypes.  

• Otic/lateral-line sensory epithelial context: pax2a, pax2b, eya1, eya4, jag2b, bdnf
→ These genes support inner-ear/lateral-line sensory-organ context. 

**Decision rule:**

The combination of mechanotransduction genes (tmc2a/tmc2b, cdh23, and pcdh15a/b), stereocilia genes (myo6b, myo7aa, myo15aa/ab/b, espn, and ptprq), ciliary/IFT genes, and ribbon-synapse machinery (otofa, slc17a8, and cacna1da) supports annotation as mature mechanosensory hair cells.

**Distinguishing note:**

This cluster is distinguished from supporting cells by the dominant mechanotransduction, stereocilia, and ribbon-synapse program. It is distinguished from CNS neurons by hair-cell-specific tip-link and stereocilia machinery, especially cdh23, pcdh15a/b, tmc2a/b, myo6b, myo7aa, myo15 genes, espn, ptprq, and otofa. The dominant signal is mature mechanosensory hair-cell identity, not generic neuronal or epithelial identity.


```{r}
DotPlot(lSeqNonLB, features = c(

    # Mechanotransduction / tip-link machinery
    "tmc1", "tmc2a", "tmc2b",
    "cdh23", "pcdh15a", "pcdh15b",
    "cabp2b", "ptprq",

    # Stereocilia / hair-bundle structure
    "myo6b", "myo7aa",
    "myo15aa", "myo15ab", "myo15b",
    "myo3b", "espn", "whrna", "ripor2", "ush1c",

    # Hair-cell ribbon synapse / neurotransmission
    "otofa", "slc17a8",
    "cacna1da", "cacna1db",
    "rims2a", "rims2b",
    "pcloa", "pclob",
    "rab3ab", "syt14a",

    # Ciliary / kinocilium and axonemal program
    "dnah5", "dnah7", "dnah9", "dnah9l", "dnah2",
    "cfap58",
    "ift172", "ift80", "ift122", "ift140",
    "dync2i1", "bbs9", "rfx2", "pacrg", "hydin",

    # Otic / lateral-line sensory epithelial context
    "pax2a", "pax2b", "eya1", "eya4", "jag2b", "bdnf"

  )
) + RotatedAxis()
```

```{r}
  group.by      = c("population", "sample_id", "celltype"),

)

coldata <- pb@meta.data %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("col_id") %>%     # rownames are the pseudo-bulk column IDs
  transmute(
    col_id     = col_id,
    sample     = sample_id,
    Population = factor(population, levels = c("surface", "cave")),
    CellType   = celltype
  )
```

### volcano check
```{r}
res_df <- res_photo %>%
   mutate(
    padj = as.numeric(padj),
    log2FoldChange_shrunk = as.numeric(log2FoldChange_shrunk),
    logP = -log10(pmax(padj, .Machine$double.xmin)),  # avoid Inf
    significance = dplyr::case_when(
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange_shrunk >  1 ~ "Up in Cave",
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange_shrunk < -1 ~ "Up in Surface",
      TRUE ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )

ggplot(res_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange_shrunk, y = logP, color = significance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Up in Cave" = "palevioletred",
    "Up in Surface" = "darkseagreen3",
    "Not significant" = "lightgray"
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano Plot: Cave vs Surface (photo)",
    x = "Shrunken log2 Fold Change (Cave vs Surface)",
    y = "-log10 Adjusted p-value",
    color = "DE Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

### Functional dot plot of DEGs
There were no significant KEGG or GO enrichment categories for this cell type so genes were grouped by functional category
```{r}
plot_pineal_photo_deg_dot <- function(
  res_all,
  title = "Pineal epithelial photoreceptors: Cave vs Surface DEGs",
  gene_col = c("final_gene_symbol","gene","Gene.Name"),
  lfc_col  = c("log2FoldChange_shrunk","log2FoldChange","lfc"),
  padj_col = c("padj","p_val_adj","pvalue","p_val"),
  direction_col = c("significance","direction"),
  only_sig = FALSE,
  padj_cut = 0.05,
  lfc_cut  = 0.5,
  top_n_per_group = 30,                 # figure density control
  drop_LOC = TRUE,
  loc_regex = "^LOC",
  colour_mode = c("viridis_abs","signed"),
  viridis_limits = c(0, 4),
  signed_limits  = c(-4, 4)
) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(dplyr)
    library(ggplot2)
    library(patchwork)
    library(scales)
    library(tibble)
  })

  colour_mode <- match.arg(colour_mode)

  # pick existing cols
  gene_col <- gene_col[gene_col %in% names(res_all)][1]
  lfc_col  <- lfc_col[lfc_col %in% names(res_all)][1]
  padj_col <- padj_col[padj_col %in% names(res_all)][1]
  direction_col <- direction_col[direction_col %in% names(res_all)][1]

  if (is.na(gene_col)) stop("No gene column found in res_all.")
  if (is.na(lfc_col) && is.na(direction_col)) stop("Need either LFC column or significance/direction column.")

  # build base
  df <- res_all %>%
    mutate(gene_label = as.character(.data[[gene_col]])) %>%
    { if (drop_LOC) filter(., !grepl(loc_regex, gene_label)) else . } %>%
    mutate(
      lfc = if (!is.na(lfc_col)) as.numeric(.data[[lfc_col]]) else NA_real_,
      Group = case_when(
        !is.na(direction_col) & grepl("Up in Cave", .data[[direction_col]], ignore.case = TRUE)    ~ "Cave",
        !is.na(direction_col) & grepl("Up in Surface", .data[[direction_col]], ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Surface",
        is.na(direction_col) & !is.na(lfc) & lfc >= 0 ~ "Cave",
        is.na(direction_col) & !is.na(lfc) & lfc <  0 ~ "Surface",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      ),
      abs_lfc = ifelse(!is.na(lfc), abs(lfc), NA_real_)
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Group))

  # padj for dot size (if present)
  if (!is.na(padj_col)) {
    df <- df %>%
      mutate(
        padj = as.numeric(.data[[padj_col]]),
        neglog10padj = -log10(pmax(padj, .Machine$double.xmin))
      )
  } else {
    df$padj <- NA_real_
    df$neglog10padj <- 1
  }

  # optional sig filter
  if (isTRUE(only_sig) && !is.na(padj_col)) {
    df <- df %>%
      filter(!is.na(padj), padj < padj_cut) %>%
      { if (!is.na(lfc_col)) filter(., abs_lfc >= lfc_cut) else . }
  }

  
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # RULE-BASED functional annotation - unannotated genes excluded
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
 
   df <- df %>%
    mutate(
      Func = case_when(
        # Phototransduction / chromophore / retinoid cycle
        grepl("^(opn|gnat|gngt|pde6|cnga|cngb|grk|arr|sag|rpe65|rlbp|lrat|rdh|rbp|rgr)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Phototransduction / retinoid",

        # Phosphoinositide / PIP metabolism
        grepl("(pip5k|pi4k|pip4p|inpp5|pitpn|dgk)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Phosphoinositide signaling",

        # MAPK / kinase signaling
        grepl("(mapk|map3k|mknk|brsk|jnk|erk|tnika|jakmip)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "MAPK / kinase signaling",

        # Ion channels / fast excitability coupling
        grepl("^(kcn|scn|cacna|chrn|gnaz$|prkar)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Fast signaling / excitability",

        # ECM / adhesion / matrix
        grepl("^(col|lama|lamc|thbs|matn|ccn|adamts|hs\\d|usta)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "ECM / matrix / adhesion",

        # Guidance / wiring (ephrins, semas, slit, ryk, etc.)
        grepl("^(sema|slit|eph|efna|cadm|cdh|igsf|lgr|gpc|nrp|unc5|plxn|ryk)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Guidance / wiring",

        # Cytoskeleton / trafficking (general)
        grepl("(map\\d|nav\\d|cep\\d|syne\\d|tmod|limch|afap|plec|dbn|kank|klc|dync)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Cytoskeleton / trafficking",

        # Myosin / actin machinery / stereocilia-related
        grepl("^(myo|myrip|espn)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Myosin / actin machinery",

        # Lipid droplets / lipid handling
        grepl("^(plin|bscl2|acsl|tm6sf|scarb|pltp|pnpla|bco2)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Lipid handling / droplets",

        # Metabolism / mitochondrial state
        grepl("(ppargc|gls\\d|pcx|bcat|mocos|aox\\d|cyb561|slc\\d)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Metabolism / transport",

        # Pigmentation / melanosome
        grepl("^(mlana|oca2|pmel|dct|tfec)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Pigmentation / melanosome",

        # Immune / myeloid-like
        grepl("^(csf1r|il\\d|scara|scarf|coro1c)", gene_label, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
          "Immune-associated",

        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Func))  # enforce: all plotted genes have a functional category

  # set ordering
  func_levels <- c(
    "Phototransduction / retinoid",
    "Phosphoinositide signaling",
    "MAPK / kinase signaling",
    "Fast signaling / excitability",
    "Guidance / wiring",
    "ECM / matrix / adhesion",
    "Cytoskeleton / trafficking",
    "Myosin / actin machinery",
    "Lipid handling / droplets",
    "Metabolism / transport",
    "Pigmentation / melanosome",
    "Immune-associated"
  )

  df <- df %>%
    mutate(
      Group = factor(Group, levels = c("Cave","Surface")),
      Func  = factor(Func, levels = func_levels)
    ) %>%
    group_by(Group) %>%
    { if (!is.null(top_n_per_group)) {
        if (!is.na(padj_col)) slice_head(arrange(., padj, desc(abs_lfc)), n = top_n_per_group)
        else slice_head(arrange(., desc(abs_lfc)), n = top_n_per_group)
      } else . } %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    arrange(Group, Func, desc(abs_lfc), if (!is.na(padj_col)) padj else Inf) %>%
    mutate(gene_label = factor(gene_label, levels = rev(unique(gene_label))))

  # colors for Func strip
  func_cols <- c(
    "Phototransduction / retinoid"     = "#3C5488",
    "Phosphoinositide signaling"       = "#E64B35",
    "MAPK / kinase signaling"          = "#F39B7F",
    "Fast signaling / excitability"    = "#B24745",
    "Guidance / wiring"                = "#5E3C99",
    "ECM / matrix / adhesion"          = "#00A087",
    "Cytoskeleton / trafficking"       = "#8491B4",
    "Myosin / actin machinery"         = "#DC0000",
    "Lipid handling / droplets"        = "#D4A72C",
    "Metabolism / transport"           = "#2E8B57",
    "Pigmentation / melanosome"        = "#7E6148",
    "Immune-associated"                = "#6A6599"
  )

  # main dot
  dot_main <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Group, y = gene_label)) +
    geom_point(
      aes(
        size  = neglog10padj,
        colour = if (colour_mode == "viridis_abs") abs_lfc else lfc
      ),
      alpha = 0.9
    ) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
    scale_size_continuous(name = expression(-log[10](padj)))

  if (colour_mode == "viridis_abs") {
    dot_main <- dot_main +
      scale_colour_viridis_c(
        name = "|log2FC|",
     #   limits = c(0,2),
        limits = viridis_limits,
        oob = scales::squish
      )
  } else {
    dot_main <- dot_main +
      scale_colour_gradient2(
        name = "log2FC (Cave vs Surface)",
        midpoint = 0,
        limits = signed_limits,
        oob = scales::squish
      )
  }

  # functional strip
  strip <- ggplot(df, aes(x = 1, y = gene_label, fill = Func)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = func_cols, drop = FALSE) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  p <- dot_main + strip +
    patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(4, 0.65), guides = "collect") &
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

  list(plot = p, df_plot = df)
}

## out$df_plot
```

## Pineal photoreceptor subset
```{r}
photo <- subset(lSeqNonCF_sub, idents = "b7")
photo$population <- factor(photo$population, levels = c("surface", "cave"))

Idents(photo) <- "population"
```
### plot for figure
```{r}
# base plot cropped to pineal range
U <- Embeddings(lSeqNonCF_sub, "umap")[Cells(photo), , drop = FALSE]
pad <- 1
xlim_use <- range(U[,1]) + c(-pad, pad)
ylim_use <- range(U[,2]) + c(-pad, pad)

p <- DimPlot(
  photo, reduction = "umap",
  group.by = "population",
  cols = c("darkseagreen3", "palevioletred"),
  shuffle = TRUE, pt.size = 3
) +
  coord_fixed() +
  xlim(xlim_use) +
  ylim(ylim_use)

# Remove axes but turn off clipping
p_clean <- p +
  theme_void() +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme(
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)  # increase if labels get cut off
  )

# Compute ranges AFTER cropping (so arrows scale correctly)
gb <- ggplot_build(p_clean)
x_rng <- gb$layout$panel_params[[1]]$x.range
y_rng <- gb$layout$panel_params[[1]]$y.range
x_span <- diff(x_rng)
y_span <- diff(y_rng)

# Position + sizing of the corner axis
axis_frac <- 0.20   # length of each axis as fraction of plot range (tune)
pad_frac  <- 0.08   # inset from corner (tune)

x0 <- x_rng[1] + pad_frac * x_span
y0 <- y_rng[1] + pad_frac * y_span
dx <- axis_frac * x_span
dy <- axis_frac * y_span

# Styling
lw <- 1.4
arrow_len <- unit(4, "mm")
label_size <- 7  # ggplot text size units

p_final <- p_clean +
  # X axis with arrow
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x0, xend = x0 + dx,
    y = y0, yend = y0,
    linewidth = lw,
    lineend = "square",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = arrow_len)
  ) +
  # Y axis with arrow
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x0, xend = x0,
    y = y0, yend = y0 + dy,
    linewidth = lw,
    lineend = "square",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = arrow_len)
  ) +
  # Labels
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x0 + dx * 0.55, y = y0 - 0.05 * y_span,
    label = "UMAP 1",
    size = label_size, fontface = "bold", vjust = 1
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x0 - 0.06 * x_span, y = y0 + dy * 0.55,
    label = "UMAP 2",
    angle = 90,
    size = label_size, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1
  )

p_final

#ggsave("photoUMAPcords.pdf", plot = p_final, width = 10, height = 10, dpi = 300)
```

#### Stats - sample level
```{r}
score_cols <- c("PhotoModule1", "FastModule1", "IntraModule1")

# Pull per-cell data including sample_id
df_sample <- FetchData(
  photo,
  vars = c("population", "sample_id", score_cols)
) %>%
  mutate(
    population = factor(population, levels = c("surface","cave"))
  )


# Collapse to SAMPLE level (mean per sample)
df_sample_means <- df_sample %>%
  group_by(sample_id, population) %>%
  summarise(
    across(all_of(score_cols), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(score_cols),
    names_to = "module",
    values_to = "mean_score"
  )

print(df_sample_means)

# Helper effect sizes (sample-level)
cliffs_delta <- function(x, y) {
  outer_cmp <- outer(x, y, FUN = "-")
  (sum(outer_cmp > 0) - sum(outer_cmp < 0)) / (length(x) * length(y))
}

cohens_d <- function(x, y) {
  nx <- length(x); ny <- length(y)
  sp <- sqrt(((nx - 1)*var(x) + (ny - 1)*var(y)) / (nx + ny - 2))
  (mean(x) - mean(y)) / sp
}


# Statistical test across samples
sample_tests <- df_sample_means %>%
  group_by(module) %>%
  summarise(
    n_surface = sum(population == "surface"),
    n_cave    = sum(population == "cave"),
    mean_surface = mean(mean_score[population == "surface"]),
    mean_cave    = mean(mean_score[population == "cave"]),
    wilcox_p = wilcox.test(mean_score ~ population, exact = FALSE)$p.value,
    t_p      = t.test(mean_score ~ population)$p.value,
    cliffs_delta = cliffs_delta(
      mean_score[population == "surface"],
      mean_score[population == "cave"]
    ),
    cohens_d = cohens_d(
      mean_score[population == "surface"],
      mean_score[population == "cave"]
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    wilcox_p_adj = p.adjust(wilcox_p, method = "BH"),
    t_p_adj      = p.adjust(t_p, method = "BH")
  )

print(sample_tests)

# Optional export
# write.csv(sample_tests, "pineal_module_sample_level_stats.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```
